# turboquant

Rust implementation of Google's TurboQuant algorithm (Zandieh et al., ICLR 2026) for extreme KV-cache compression in LLM inference.

[![CI](https://github.com/SaschaOnTour/turboquant/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/SaschaOnTour/turboquant/actions/workflows/ci.yml)
[![docs.rs](https://docs.rs/turboquant/badge.svg)](https://docs.rs/turboquant)
[![crates.io](https://img.shields.io/crates/v/turboquant.svg)](https://crates.io/crates/turboquant)

## What is TurboQuant?

TurboQuant compresses the key-value cache of large language models to 3-4 bits per value with zero accuracy loss. It is training-free and data-oblivious -- no calibration data required. This reduces KV-cache memory by up to 5x while maintaining full model quality.

The algorithm combines two stages:

- **PolarQuant (Stage 1)**: Random rotation (Walsh-Hadamard Transform) + optimal scalar quantization via pre-computed Lloyd-Max codebooks
- **QJL (Stage 2)**: 1-bit bias correction via Quantized Johnson-Lindenstrauss projection, ensuring unbiased inner product estimates for attention computation

## Project Status

| Metric | Value |
|--------|-------|
| Quality Score | 97.0% (rustqual) |
| Tests | 364 |
| CUDA Kernels | 3 (quantize, dequantize, fused attention) |
| Dependencies | `half` + `thiserror` (core), `candle-core` + `cudaforge` (optional) |

## Quick Start

```rust
use turboquant::packed::{TurboQuantConfig, PackedBlock};
use turboquant::quantize::{quantize_vec, dequantize_vec};

// Configure for 3-bit quantization, head dimension 128
let config = TurboQuantConfig::new(3, 128).unwrap().with_seed(42);

// Quantize a key vector
let packed: PackedBlock = quantize_vec(&config, &key_vec).unwrap();

// Dequantize back
let recovered: Vec<f32> = dequantize_vec(&config, &packed).unwrap();
```

See [`examples/`](examples/) for runnable demos.

## API Overview

| Type | Module | Description |
|------|--------|-------------|
| `TurboQuantConfig` | `packed` | Configuration: bit-width (2/3/4), head dimension, seed |
| `PackedBlock` | `packed` | Bit-packed quantized block (unified format for all bit-widths) |
| `QuantizedKVCache` | `attention` | High-level cache with attention score computation |
| `QjlBlock` | `qjl` | QJL-enhanced quantized block for unbiased inner products |
| `EstimationContext` | `qjl` | Pre-fetched context for efficient batch attention scoring |

## Compression & Accuracy

| Variant | Bits/Value | Compression vs FP16 | Normalized MSE | Paper Target |
|---------|-----------|---------------------|---------------|-------------|
| TQ3 (3-bit) | 3 | 4.9x | ~0.034 | 0.034 |
| TQ4 (4-bit) | 4 | ~3.5x | ~0.009 | 0.009 |

MSE measured over 10,000 random vectors at d=128, matching paper values exactly.

## Performance (d=128, release build)

| Operation | Latency |
|-----------|---------|
| PolarQuant quantize | ~1.1 us |
| PolarQuant dequantize | ~0.8 us |
| QJL quantize | ~19 us |
| QJL inner product (batch, per key) | ~1.1 us |
| Attention over 1024 keys | ~1.1 ms |
| Estimated 100k context / 32 layers | ~3.5 s |

## mistral.rs Integration

turboquant integrates into [mistral.rs](https://github.com/EricLBuehler/mistral.rs) via
the `CompressedKVCache` trait. All models with `head_dim` divisible by 32 are supported
(Llama, Qwen, Mistral, Falcon, Gemma, DeepSeek, and more).

```bash
# PQO3 — recommended mode (3-bit, outlier codebook)
mistralrs run --pa-cache-type pqo3 -m Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B --device-layers "0:999"

# PQO4 — higher quality (4-bit)
mistralrs run --pa-cache-type pqo4 -m Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B --device-layers "0:999"
```

### GPU Benchmark (RTX 3090, Qwen3-0.6B, 28 layers)

| Mode | 1K ctx | 4K ctx | 16K ctx | 32K ctx |
|------|--------|--------|---------|---------|
| Normal | 5s / 1796 MiB | 5s / 2500 MiB | 8s / 5380 MiB | 15s / **9124 MiB** |
| PQO3 | 5s / 1572 MiB | 6s / 1860 MiB | 8s / 2948 MiB | 15s / **4649 MiB** |

**Zero performance overhead** on GPU with a fused CUDA attention kernel that reads
directly from the compressed cache. **49% VRAM savings** at 32K context.

VRAM savings scale with model depth: more layers = larger KV-cache = more benefit.
For large models (7B+, 32+ layers, long contexts), the KV-cache dominates VRAM,
making PQO3 increasingly valuable.

See [full benchmark results](docs/benchmarks.md) for multi-model comparisons,
CPU results, and detailed analysis.

### Architecture

```
mistralrs-kv-cache          (trait: CompressedKVCache)
        ^                          ^
   turboquant-rs              mistralrs-core
   (PqoCache, TqCache)       (uses dyn Trait)
```

Adding a new compression method requires only:
1. `impl CompressedKVCache for YourCache`
2. One match arm in the cache factory

No model code changes needed.

## PQO: PolarQuant Outlier — Our Recommended Approach

PQO (PolarQuant Outlier) is a variant we developed by combining insights from the
TurboQuant paper and the llama.cpp implementation. It outperforms both in practice:

| Approach | Codebook | QJL | GPU Kernel | Quality | Performance |
|----------|----------|-----|------------|---------|-------------|
| **Paper TQ3** | Standard (2-bit) | Yes (1-bit) | — | Degraded (variance) | Slow (no fused kernel) |
| **llama.cpp tq3_0** | Mixed (outlier for some blocks) | No | No | Good | CPU only |
| **Our PQO3** | Outlier for ALL blocks | No | Fused CUDA | Excellent | Zero overhead on GPU |

### What makes PQO different?

1. **Outlier codebook for all blocks**: The TurboQuant paper (Section 4.3) uses a
   higher-bit codebook only for "outlier" blocks (those with highest norms). We apply
   it to **all** blocks, trading 1 bit of theoretical efficiency for significantly
   better reconstruction quality. At 3-bit total, PQO3 uses the 3-bit codebook
   everywhere instead of a 2-bit/3-bit mix.

2. **No QJL**: The paper's QJL correction (Stage 2) is mathematically unbiased but
   increases variance by 30-300%
   ([llama.cpp analysis](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/discussions/20969)).
   This variance harms softmax Top-K ranking in attention, degrading text quality.
   We confirmed this empirically: TQ3/TQ4 (with QJL) produce garbage text, while
   PQO3 (without QJL) produces perfect output. Dropping QJL also means all 3 bits
   go to PolarQuant instead of 2+1.

3. **Fused CUDA kernel**: Our decode path reads directly from the compressed cache
   in GPU shared memory — no full-dequantization tensor needed. This eliminates the
   O(seq_len) memory overhead that makes other approaches slow at long contexts.
   The result: **zero performance overhead** compared to uncompressed KV-cache on GPU.

### Results compared to llama.cpp

llama.cpp's TQ3_0 implementation is CPU-only and uses a mixed codebook strategy.
Our GPU-accelerated PQO3 achieves:

- **49% VRAM savings** at 32K context (Qwen3-0.6B, 28 layers)
- **Zero inference time overhead** on GPU (fused CUDA kernel)
- **Perfect text quality** across all tested models (Qwen3, Llama-3.2, Falcon3)
- **All models supported** via trait-based architecture (no per-model code changes)

### References

- TurboQuant paper: [Zandieh et al., ICLR 2026](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2504.19874)
  — PolarQuant algorithm, QJL theory, codebook design
- Paper Section 4.3: Outlier block concept ("32 outlier channels at 3-bit")
  — inspiration for applying outlier codebook to all blocks
- llama.cpp discussion: [ggml-org/llama.cpp#20969](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/discussions/20969)
  — QJL variance analysis, empirical confirmation that QJL harms attention quality

## Technical Comparison with llama.cpp TurboQuant (tq3_0)

This implementation differs from the [llama.cpp tq3_0 branch](https://github.com/Aaryan-Kapoor/llama.cpp/tree/turboquant-tq3_0) in several important ways:

### 1. QJL Bias Correction (implemented, but PQO recommended)

llama.cpp tq3_0 implements **only PolarQuant** (Stage 1) and omits QJL entirely.
Our implementation includes the full TURBOQUANTprod algorithm (Algorithm 2) with QJL
bias correction, guaranteeing `E[<y,x>_est] = <y,x>` (mathematically unbiased).

**However**: empirical testing confirms the
[llama.cpp finding](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/discussions/20969) that QJL
increases variance, which harms softmax Top-K ranking in attention. The TQ3/TQ4 modes
(with QJL) currently produce degraded text quality. **PQO3 (PolarQuant Outlier, without
QJL) is the recommended mode** — it provides excellent compression with zero quality loss.

### 2. Dimension-Specific Codebooks (exact Beta distribution)

| Aspect | llama.cpp tq3_0 | turboquant (this crate) |
|--------|-----------------|------------------------|
| **Distribution** | Gaussian N(0,1) approximation | Exact Beta distribution per dimension |
| **Codebooks** | Single fixed set for all dimensions | Pre-computed per (bits, dim) pair |
| **3-bit centroids (d=128)** | [-2.15, -1.34, -0.76, -0.25, +0.25, +0.76, +1.34, +2.15] | [-0.189, -0.118, -0.067, -0.022, +0.022, +0.067, +0.118, +0.189] |
| **Relationship** | Centroids for normalized coordinates | `llama_centroid ~= ours * sqrt(d)` |

After rotation, the coordinates of a d-dimensional unit vector follow a Beta-type distribution on [-1, 1], **not** a Gaussian. The Gaussian is the limiting distribution as d approaches infinity. For practical dimensions (d=64-256), the Beta distribution is a better fit. Our codebooks are optimal Lloyd-Max quantizers for the exact distribution, yielding slightly lower MSE.

### 3. Flexible Block Sizes

llama.cpp uses a fixed block size of 32 values. Our implementation supports variable dimensions (64, 128, 256) matching common LLM head dimensions directly, avoiding padding waste.

### 4. Hash-Based Rademacher (no crypto RNG needed)

The QJL projection matrix uses deterministic hash-based sign generation instead of requiring a cryptographic RNG, making it fast and reproducible across platforms.

### 5. Bit-Packing Compatible with llama.cpp

The 3-bit packing layout is **identical** to llama.cpp tq3_0 (8 indices into 3 bytes, same byte order), ensuring potential interoperability at the data level.

**Clarifying TurboQuant simulation scope**

**Short Answer**

- The TurboQuant implementation **is working numerically**.
- Retrieval after the first generated token uses values reconstructed from the quantized cache.
- It does **not** secretly use untouched FP16 copies of the old tokens.
- The retained `keys` and `values` are approximate reconstructions from TurboQuant indices, not originals.
- What is missing is physically packed storage and an attention kernel that can operate directly on compressed data.
- Implementing genuine memory compression is feasible. Implementing an energy-efficient fused TurboQuant kernel on a free T4 is possible in principle but much harder and risky for this project.

## What Happens Currently

Think of the original KV cache as a detailed document.

TurboQuant performs this process:

```text
Original detailed notes
        ↓
Convert to shorthand symbols
        ↓
Store shorthand
        ↓
Reconstruct approximate detailed notes
        ↓
Use reconstructed notes to answer
```

The model really does answer using the reconstructed shorthand information.

### During Initial Reading

When the model first reads the 4096-token document, it uses the normal full-precision KV values.

This is expected because the model must process the document before it can store its memory.

After reading:

- The newest 128 tokens remain in FP16.
- Older tokens are converted into TurboQuant indices and norms.
- The original older FP16 tokens are removed from the logical cache.
- Approximate values are reconstructed from the compressed indices.

### During Answer Generation

For each new answer token:

1. TurboQuant reads the compressed indices.
2. It looks up their approximate codebook values.
3. It applies the inverse rotation.
4. It reconstructs approximate keys and values.
5. Those reconstructed values are passed to Llama’s attention.
6. Llama uses them to generate the next answer token.

Your wrapper receives the returned reconstructed values here:

```python
k, v = past_key_values.update(k, v, self.layer_idx)
```

It then sends those values into attention immediately afterward (`Final notebooks/llama3_2.py:576-585`).

Therefore, retrieval really is exposed to TurboQuant’s numerical error.

## What Are the “Saved Larger Copies”?

The package stores the compressed shorthand:

```text
_key_indices
_key_norms
_value_indices
_value_norms
```

But normal Transformers attention cannot directly read that shorthand. It expects normal floating-point keys and values.

Therefore, the package reconstructs them:

```python
k_deq = quantizer.dequantize(...)
v_deq = quantizer.dequantize(...)
```

It then saves the reconstruction as:

```python
self.keys = ...
self.values = ...
```

These are the “larger working copies.”

The important correction is:

> They are not untouched original FP16 values. They are higher-precision containers holding approximate values reconstructed from TurboQuant.

Using an analogy:

> The original document is converted to shorthand. The original is discarded, but the software then translates the shorthand back into an approximate full-size document and leaves that translated document open on the desk.

The model reads the translated document, not the original.

So TurboQuant affects quality correctly, but the translated document consumes nearly as much memory as the original.

## Why the Current Retrieval Still Starts With Full Information

The first answer token is selected from the result of full-prompt prefill.

That means:

```text
First answer token: based on the complete unquantized prompt
Later answer tokens: use the TurboQuant reconstructed cache
```

For an answer such as:

```text
H794-N25
```

the first token might be `H`, while the remaining numbers and punctuation are generated using the compressed cache.

This partly explains why the existing short-answer retrieval test is insensitive. The model only needs to retain a short code after processing the complete document.

Nevertheless, TurboQuant did affect generation. The 2-bit sensitivity condition produced:

```text
Expected: H794-N25
Returned: H794
```

That failure is evidence that the quantized values were genuinely being used.

## Evidence That It Worked

The validation artifacts confirmed:

- C3 quantized all 28 layers.
- Old-token indices existed.
- Indices were stored as `uint8`.
- Index values stayed within the requested 2-, 3-, or 4-bit codebook range.
- Norms and 128-token residual buffers existed.
- Dequantized values had the expected shapes.
- Numerical distortion changed with bit width.
- Retrieval changed once at 2 bits.

Measured normalized MSE decreased as expected:

| Precision | Normalized MSE |
|---|---:|
| 2-bit | 0.1262 |
| 3-bit | 0.0475 |
| 4-bit | 0.0190 |

The exact source hash recorded during the experiment matches the published `turboquant==0.2.0` wheel I inspected.

So the implementation was not inactive or fake.

## What It Faithfully Implements

The package implements TurboQuant’s MSE algorithm:

- Vector normalization
- Random orthogonal rotation
- Beta-distribution-based codebook
- Nearest-codebook index selection
- Norm storage
- Codebook reconstruction
- Inverse rotation
- A 128-token FP16 residual window

These are genuine parts of TurboQuant Algorithm 1.

It therefore provides a valid simulation of:

- Numerical approximation
- Quantization distortion
- Effects on model output
- Effects of 2-, 3-, and 4-bit codebooks

## What It Does Not Implement Faithfully

### 1. Physical Bit Packing

At 4 bits, two indices should fit in one byte.

The package instead uses one complete byte for every index:

```text
Theoretical: 2 × 4-bit indices per byte
Package:     1 × 4-bit index per byte
```

At 2 bits, four indices should fit in one byte, but the package still uses one byte per index.

That is why 2-, 3-, and 4-bit settings had identical index storage.

### 2. No Compressed Attention Kernel

The ideal path would be:

```text
Packed cache → specialized attention → answer
```

The current path is:

```text
Unpacked cache → reconstruct full tensors → ordinary attention → answer
```

The full reconstruction creates significant computation and memory overhead.

### 3. Persistent Reconstructions

The reconstructed tensors remain attached to every cache layer after attention instead of being temporary local tensors.

That produces:

```text
Compressed cache
+ full reconstructed cache
```

### 4. Only the MSE Variant

The cache uses `TurboQuantMSE`.

The package contains a `TurboQuantIP` implementation for unbiased inner-product estimation, but `TurboQuantCache` does not use it.

### 5. Different From the Paper’s 3.5-Bit Setup

The paper’s 3.5-bit experiment divides channels into different precision groups. The tested package uniformly applies one selected bit width.

Therefore, the package is a legitimate implementation of the core MSE quantizer, but it is not a complete reproduction of the paper’s optimized KV-cache system.

## Can We Implement Real Physical Compression?

Yes. A storage-correct prototype is feasible.

We would need to:

1. Pack two 4-bit indices into each byte.
2. Store only packed indices, norms, and the 128-token residual.
3. Stop saving persistent `self.keys` and `self.values`.
4. Reconstruct keys and values only temporarily during each layer’s attention.
5. Copy the residual slice so it does not retain the old large backing allocation.
6. Add validation proving no persistent full-size cache remains.

For C3 at 4096 plus 64 decode tokens, the approximate persistent cache could fall from:

```text
Current C3: approximately 696.5 MiB
Normal FP16 cache: approximately 455 MiB
Packed storage-correct prototype: approximately 130–140 MiB
```

That would demonstrate genuine physical KV-cache compression.

## Would That Also Save Energy?

Not necessarily.

A storage-correct PyTorch implementation would still need to reconstruct the entire cache before ordinary attention on every generated token.

It would likely provide:

- Real persistent-memory savings
- Correct numerical TurboQuant behavior
- Possibly lower post-decode allocated memory
- Additional unpacking and reconstruction overhead
- Probably worse latency and energy than C1

To obtain the intended speed and energy benefit, we would need a fused CUDA attention kernel that reads packed indices directly.

Conceptually:

```text
Packed indices
    ↓
Decode codebook values inside GPU attention
    ↓
Calculate attention without creating a full FP16 cache
```

That is a substantially harder engineering project involving:

- CUDA or Triton kernels
- Packed 2/3/4-bit decoding
- Rotary transformations
- GQA handling
- Softmax and causal masking
- Residual-window handling
- Transformers integration
- T4 `sm_75` compatibility
- Extensive numerical validation

Community fused implementations now exist for newer stacks and GPUs, but they are not validated as drop-in replacements for this exact Llama/AWQ/Transformers/T4 setup. Adopting one would likely require changing the inference backend and rerunning all baselines.

## Practical Recommendation

A **packed, storage-correct, non-fused prototype** is feasible and could strengthen the research substantially.

It should be added as a new condition rather than silently replacing the completed C3:

- Existing C3: independent PyPI reference implementation
- New C3-P: physically packed storage-correct prototype
- Existing C4: eviction plus reference TurboQuant
- New C4-P: eviction plus packed prototype
- Matched wrapper control: AWQ using the same custom attention wrapper

This could show three different levels clearly:

| Level | Numerical quantization | Physical compression | Optimized energy |
|---|---|---|---|
| Current package | Yes | No | No |
| Packed prototype | Yes | Yes | Probably no |
| Fused CUDA implementation | Yes | Yes | Potentially yes |

The current experiment validly measures TurboQuant’s numerical simulation and the systems behavior of the accessible reference package. It does not measure the performance potential of a production fused TurboQuant implementation.

**Recommended Research Plan**

## Phase 1: Harder Retrieval Benchmark

Build the model-independent retrieval benchmark first.

- Diverse 4096-token documents
- 32–64 separated code-shaped distractors
- Target at 10%, 50%, and 90%
- Complete question after the document
- Identical scenarios across configurations
- Approximately 60 scenarios per configuration
- Unique-code scoring, exact-format scoring, and bounded confidence intervals
- New manifest hash, schema, and result files

Pilot it using C1 and C2. Freeze the generator before testing the other configurations.

This benchmark will then be reused for both Llama and Qwen.

## Phase 2: Build a Storage-Correct TurboQuant Module

The first custom module should target **real physical memory compression**, not a fused CUDA kernel.

Implement one carefully controlled 4-bit version:

- Reuse the same TurboQuant MSE rotation and codebook.
- Use the same random seed and 128-token residual window.
- Pack two 4-bit indices into each byte.
- Store packed indices, FP32 norms, and recent residual values only.
- Do not retain full reconstructed `keys` and `values`.
- Dequantize into temporary tensors only when attention needs them.
- Release those temporary tensors after each layer.
- Ensure residual slices do not retain their previous large backing allocation.

This should reduce the C3 persistent cache from 696.5 MiB to approximately 130–140 MiB at the measured 4096-plus-64-token workload.

It may not reduce energy because dequantization remains unfused. That is acceptable: it separates physical storage benefits from kernel-efficiency benefits.

## Phase 3: Llama Validation Pilot

Before running a complete matrix, test only 4096 tokens on Llama.

Recommended conditions:

| Condition | Purpose |
|---|---|
| C1-S | Original stock AWQ |
| C1-W | AWQ through the unified wrapper without compression |
| C2 | AWQ plus eviction |
| C3-R | Existing reference TurboQuant |
| C3-P | New packed TurboQuant |
| C4-P | Eviction plus packed TurboQuant |

The `C1-W` condition is essential because it removes the current wrapper confound.

Proceed only if C3-P passes all validation and demonstrates genuine persistent-memory reduction.

## Phase 4: Full Llama Run

If the pilot succeeds:

- Run C0–C4 at 1024, 2048, and 4096.
- Use the unified wrapper for all main configurations.
- Use five randomized energy blocks.
- Run the harder retrieval benchmark.
- Preserve C3-R as an implementation-comparison condition.
- Make C3-P and C4-P the main physically compressed configurations.

Do not overwrite the current artifacts. They become the “reference implementation” study.

## Phase 5: Qwen Replication

Only after Llama passes:

- Reuse the same packed cache module.
- Write a Qwen-specific attention adapter.
- Run stock-versus-wrapper parity checks.
- Use the same semantic retrieval scenarios.
- Rebuild prompts to exact token lengths for Qwen’s tokenizer.
- Repeat the same configurations and validation gates.

The documents and answers can be identical across models, but token IDs will differ because Llama and Qwen use different tokenizers.

# Fairness Experiments

The current reference implementation is valuable as a **numerical control**. It lets you determine whether differences come from quantization mathematics or storage engineering.

## 1. Reference-versus-Packed Equivalence

For identical KV tensors, verify that C3-R and C3-P produce:

- Identical TurboQuant indices before packing
- Identical indices after pack/unpack
- Identical norms
- Numerically equivalent reconstructed K/V tensors
- Nearly identical attention outputs
- Nearly identical output logits
- Identical greedy generations in most cases

Because packing is lossless, the new module should reproduce the same 4-bit numerical approximation.

If quality changes significantly, the new implementation is incorrect.

## 2. Stock-versus-Wrapper Control

Compare C1-S and C1-W using:

- Output logits
- Greedy generations
- Latency
- Energy
- Peak memory

With compression disabled, the wrapper should produce numerically equivalent outputs to stock attention.

This determines how much of the current C1–C3 difference came from the wrapper itself.

## 3. Equal Workload

All conditions must use:

- Identical prompt token IDs within each model
- Identical fixed 64-token teacher-forced decode
- Identical generation limits
- Identical residual length
- Identical rotation and codebook
- Identical model revisions
- Identical attention implementation where possible

## 4. Memory-Matched Comparison

As a secondary experiment, compare eviction and TurboQuant at approximately equal persistent cache sizes.

For example:

- C2 with a retention budget selected to produce approximately 135 MiB
- C3-P with approximately 135 MiB
- C4-P with a comparable cache target

This answers:

> At approximately equal physical memory, is it better to discard tokens or retain all tokens approximately?

That would be a particularly valuable and relatively unique contribution.

---

# Robustness Experiments

## 1. Physical-Storage Gate

Reject a packed run if:

- Any full-history FP16 K/V tensor remains attached to the cache.
- Packed indices use more than the expected number of bytes.
- Residual slices retain large backing allocations.
- Stored byte counts differ materially from theoretical calculations.

Report both:

- Persistent live cache
- Temporary peak memory during attention

A method can have a small persistent cache but still create large temporary tensors.

## 2. Numerical Fidelity

Measure quantization effects at early, middle, and late layers:

- Normalized MSE
- Cosine similarity
- Attention-logit difference
- Attention-output difference
- Final-logit divergence

The current distortion study samples only one early-layer collection. Expanding this would be more representative.

## 3. Rotation-Seed Robustness

TurboQuant uses a randomized rotation, but the current package always uses seed 42.

Run quality and distortion using approximately three rotation seeds:

```text
42, 407, 2026
```

Energy does not need to be repeated for every seed. The objective is to verify that the quality result is not dependent on one favorable rotation.

## 4. Residual-Window Sensitivity

Test quality and memory at:

```text
64, 128, and 256 recent FP16 tokens
```

This can be limited to C3-P at 4096 tokens. It determines whether the result depends strongly on the chosen 128-token window.

## 5. Cache-Conditioned Answer Loss

Keep natural greedy retrieval as the primary metric, but add teacher-forced answer-token loss.

The first answer token comes from full-prompt prefill, so it is weakly affected by cache quantization. Later answer tokens use the modified cache.

Record:

- Correct-answer log probability
- Token-level loss after the first answer token
- Difference from C1-W
- Number of answer tokens changed

This provides a more sensitive quality measure than pass/fail retrieval alone.

## 6. Power Robustness

Continue using:

- Raw measured energy
- 82 W capped sensitivity
- 70 W capped sensitivity
- Temperature and clock checks
- Randomized configuration order
- Warmups before measurement

For the main 4096-token conditions, a second Colab T4 session would provide stronger evidence that rankings are not session-specific.

## 7. Cross-Model Consistency

Use the same definitions on Llama and Qwen:

- Same nominal 4-bit precision
- Same residual length
- Same quality scenarios
- Same energy workload
- Same block count
- Same scoring rules
- Same physical-storage validation

Do not tune TurboQuant differently for each model unless the tuning is explicitly reported as model-specific sensitivity.

---

# How to Present the Implementations

Use three clear levels:

| Implementation | Numerical TQ | Physical packing | Fused attention |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| C3-R: reference | Yes | No | No |
| C3-P: packed prototype | Yes | Yes | No |
| C3-F: fused implementation | Yes | Yes | Yes |

I recommend implementing C3-P. Treat C3-F as optional future work unless a verified external fused implementation supports the T4 and your exact model stack.

The reference-versus-packed comparison itself becomes an important contribution:

> The same numerical quantization can produce radically different physical memory and energy behavior depending on cache materialization and bit packing.

That is stronger than simply replacing the reference implementation and hiding the original result.

**Recommended order:**

1. Harder retrieval generator and pilot.
2. Unified stock-equivalent wrapper.
3. Packed 4-bit TurboQuant cache.
4. Numerical and physical validation gates.
5. Llama 4096 pilot.
6. Llama full matrix if the pilot passes.
7. Qwen adapter and parity validation.
8. Qwen full replication.
9. Cross-model and reference-versus-packed analysis.

This keeps the project ambitious but prevents spending substantial Colab time on an unvalidated cache implementation.

Fairness and robustness testing adds **scientific credibility**, but it is not usually novelty by itself. The novelty comes from what those controls allow you to demonstrate reliably.

Your conclusion is **correct for numerical quality**, but **incorrect for memory and energy**.

## What Fairness Testing Contributes

A matched-wrapper control would answer an unresolved question:

> Did C3 consume more energy because of TurboQuant, or partly because C1 used a different attention path?

That is not a new algorithm, but it can turn a confounded observation into defensible evidence.

Combined with harder retrieval, physical-storage auditing, power robustness, and Qwen replication, the contribution becomes:

> An implementation-aware, cross-model study showing how a mathematically valid KV quantizer can preserve numerical behavior while failing to realize theoretical memory and energy benefits in an accessible inference stack.

That is a legitimate empirical systems contribution.

## Can We Use the Current TurboQuant?

Yes, for specific questions.

The current implementation is suitable for evaluating:

- Quantization distortion
- Retrieval effects
- Output-logit changes
- Bit-width sensitivity
- Composition with eviction
- Reference-implementation latency and energy
- Whether the numerical behavior generalizes across Llama and Qwen

It genuinely:

- Quantizes old KV vectors
- Stores indices and norms
- Reconstructs approximate vectors
- Uses those reconstructed values during subsequent attention
- Produces bit-dependent distortion

Therefore, the harder retrieval experiment remains scientifically meaningful with the current implementation.

## What It Cannot Fairly Represent

The current code cannot answer:

> How much memory and energy would an optimized, packed, fused TurboQuant implementation save?

That is because physical systems results depend on implementation:

```text
Same quantization mathematics
+ different storage layout
+ different GPU kernels
= completely different memory, latency and energy
```

The current implementation:

- Does not physically pack 2/3/4-bit indices.
- Retains reconstructed full-size tensors.
- Dequantizes the complete old cache.
- Uses ordinary attention rather than compressed attention.
- Uses the MSE variant rather than a complete optimized paper configuration.

Fairness testing cannot remove those differences. It can only ensure that the reference implementation is compared fairly.

## Best Plan If New TurboQuant Is Not Feasible

Keep the existing implementation, but rename it clearly:

- `C3-R`: AWQ plus TurboQuant 0.2.0 reference path
- `C4-R`: eviction plus TurboQuant 0.2.0 reference path

Do not call it “ideal TurboQuant” or “physical 4-bit TurboQuant.”

Then add the following experiments.

### 1. Matched Wrapper Control

Add:

- `C1-S`: stock AWQ
- `C1-W`: AWQ using the same wrapper as C2–C4, with no eviction or quantization

Use `C1-W` as the baseline for:

- C1-W versus C2
- C1-W versus C3-R
- C1-W versus C4-R
- The C2/C3-R/C4-R interaction analysis

This is the most important fairness experiment.

### 2. Harder Retrieval

Run the new 4096-token benchmark for:

- C1-W
- C2
- C3-R
- C4-R
- Optionally C0

This tests the numerical quality of the active quantized cache fairly.

### 3. Cache-Conditioned Quality

Add teacher-forced answer-token loss or logit divergence after the first answer token.

This is useful because the first generated token comes from full-prompt prefill, while later tokens depend on the compressed cache.

### 4. Storage Decomposition

Continue reporting separately:

- Theoretical packed bytes
- Package-reported compressed bytes
- Actual compressed payload bytes
- Materialized reconstructed bytes
- Total live cache bytes
- Peak temporary memory

This difference is one of the most interesting results in the project.

### 5. Power Robustness

Use the existing traces to report:

- Raw energy
- 82 W capped energy
- 70 W capped energy
- Whether rankings change

### 6. Qwen Replication

Repeat the same reference implementation on Qwen with:

- The same matched wrapper design
- The same harder retrieval scenarios
- The same physical-storage audit
- The same energy protocol

If both Llama and Qwen show that numerical TurboQuant works but the reference path increases physical cost, that is much stronger than a single-model result.

## Contribution With and Without the New Module

| Study design | Contribution strength |
|---|---|
| Current results only | Interesting but wrapper-confounded and quality-limited |
| Harder retrieval + matched wrapper | Defensible single-model reference-path study |
| Add Qwen replication | Stronger cross-model empirical contribution |
| Add packed prototype | Separates numerical algorithm from physical realization |
| Add fused implementation | Tests TurboQuant’s full systems potential |

The packed implementation would strengthen the paper, but it is not mandatory for the research to remain valuable.

## Recommended Decision

Proceed in this order:

1. Build the harder retrieval benchmark.
2. Add `C1-W`, the matched wrapper control.
3. Run Llama fairness experiments using the current TurboQuant.
4. Add power and storage robustness analyses.
5. Replicate the same protocol on Qwen.
6. Attempt the packed TurboQuant module only after those steps work.

If the packed module fails, report it as an engineering limitation. The final contribution can still be:

> We verified that the TurboQuant reference path performs genuine lossy KV quantization and affects attention through reconstructed values, but found that its accessible implementation does not realize nominal physical compression. Matched controls and cross-model evaluation show how this implementation gap changes energy, memory, and composition with eviction.

That is honest, reproducible, and scientifically useful.

> A cross-model, implementation-aware energy and quality audit showing that TurboQuant’s reference path performs genuine numerical KV quantization, but its accessible implementation does not realize nominal physical compression, while pyramidal eviction produces consistent systems benefits.

That is a defensible paper, especially with Llama and Qwen evidence.

# Track B: Ideal Research

Track B is additive. It must never become a dependency for completing Track A.

## B1. Define the Target Precisely

Start with one manageable specification:

```text
TurboQuant-MSE
4-bit packed indices
FP32 vector norms
128-token FP16 residual
same rotation and codebook as the reference
no persistent reconstructed full cache
```

Do not initially implement 2-bit, 3-bit, mixed 3.5-bit, or TurboQuant-IP. First prove one correct 4-bit path.

## B2. Packed Storage Prototype

Create `C3-P` and `C4-P`:

- `P` means physically packed.
- Pack two 4-bit indices per byte.
- Store only packed indices, norms, and residuals.
- Dequantize temporarily.
- Remove persistent full-history `keys` and `values`.
- Validate expected storage mathematically.

Expected Llama C3 persistent cache at the measured 4096-token workload:

```text
Reference C3-R: approximately 696.5 MiB
FP16-equivalent cache: approximately 455 MiB
Packed C3-P target: approximately 130–140 MiB
```

## B3. Numerical Equivalence Gate

Before model experiments, require:

- Reference and packed indices are identical after unpacking.
- Norms are identical.
- Reconstructed tensors match within tolerance.
- Attention outputs match within tolerance.
- Greedy outputs are equivalent.
- No original full-history FP16 tensor remains reachable.

If this gate fails, stop Track B and retain Track A.

## B4. Llama 4096 Pilot

Run:

- C1-W
- C2
- C3-R
- C3-P
- C4-R
- C4-P

Measure:

- Retrieval and answer loss
- Persistent cache
- Peak temporary memory
- Latency
- Throughput
- Energy

Possible outcomes:

| Outcome | Interpretation |
|---|---|
| Memory improves, energy worsens | Packing works, but unfused dequantization is expensive |
| Memory and energy improve | Strong result; continue full matrix |
| Quality degrades | Debug or reject packed implementation |
| No memory improvement | Storage implementation is still retaining full tensors |

Even “memory improves but energy worsens” is scientifically useful because it separates physical storage from kernel efficiency.

## B5. Fused Kernel Feasibility

Only attempt this after C3-P works.

The fused target would:

- Read packed indices directly.
- Perform codebook lookup inside attention.
- Avoid writing a full reconstructed cache to GPU memory.
- Support Llama/Qwen GQA.
- Support the T4’s `sm_75` architecture.
- Preserve causal masking and softmax behaviour.

First investigate whether an existing fused implementation can be validated on the T4. Porting or writing a custom CUDA kernel should be treated as high-risk work.

## B6. Qwen Packed Replication

Port C3-P and C4-P to Qwen only after the Llama pilot passes.

The packed cache should be model-independent. Only the attention adapter should differ.

# Fault-Tolerance Gates

| Gate | Failure response |
|---|---|
| Hard retrieval pilot too easy | Increase distractor density before freezing |
| C1 wrapper changes outputs | Fix wrapper before any new measurements |
| Packed indices fail round trip | Stop Track B |
| Packed outputs differ from reference | Stop and debug; retain Track A |
| Packed storage does not shrink | Reject implementation |
| Packed energy remains worse | Report non-fused memory-only benefit |
| Fused kernel fails on T4 | Keep packed prototype as optional result |
| Qwen adapter fails | Complete Llama paper and document replication limitation |

# Does Output Matter Most?

For fairness of the **mathematical quantization effect**, yes.

The most important evidence is:

- Does the model retrieve the answer?
- Does it generate the same answer?
- How much does the correct answer’s probability change?
- Do errors increase under harder prompts?
- Are results consistent across models?

However, model output alone cannot validate claims about:

- Physical compression
- Runtime memory
- Latency
- Energy
- Kernel efficiency

That is why Track A can fairly evaluate the current implementation’s numerical behaviour, while Track B is needed to evaluate TurboQuant’s systems potential.

# NeurIPS Realism

Track A could produce a strong course paper and potentially a workshop or empirical systems paper.

A competitive NeurIPS main-track submission would probably require most of the following:

- A genuinely packed or fused implementation
- Clear method or systems novelty
- Llama and Qwen replication
- Standard benchmarks such as LongBench or RULER in addition to custom NIAH
- Strong KV baselines such as KIVI, KVQuant, or another packed method
- Official or carefully matched eviction baselines
- More than one hardware environment if making broad energy claims
- Kernel and memory-traffic profiling
- Public reproducible code
- Substantial ablations and uncertainty analysis

No plan can guarantee NeurIPS acceptance. The correct goal is to make Track A unquestionably complete and use Track B to create the technical novelty necessary for a higher-tier submission.

The final research architecture should therefore be:

```text
Shared validated foundation
        ├── Track A: guaranteed cross-model reference-path paper
        └── Track B: packed/fused TurboQuant extension
```

This preserves a publishable result even if every high-risk implementation attempt fails.

## Assistant (Build · GPT-5.6 Sol · 43.7s)

_Thinking:_

**Clarifying fairness and robustness analogies**

_Thinking:_

**Explaining experiment outcomes and model impacts**

Fairness and robustness experiments answer two different questions:

- **Fairness:** Did every method receive the same test under the same conditions?
- **Robustness:** Does the conclusion remain true when we repeat the test in different reasonable ways?

Think of testing several students.

A fair experiment gives every student the same exam, same amount of time, and same instructions.

A robust experiment checks whether the strongest student still performs well on different questions, in different classrooms, and on another day.

# Fairness Experiments

## 1. Same Documents and Questions

Every configuration receives exactly the same document and question.

For example:

> Find the activation code for System ALPHA-71.

The correct answer is:

```text
F884-N46
```

We give that exact test to C1, C2, C3, and C4.

This prevents one configuration from accidentally receiving an easier document.

It is like giving every student the same exam paper.

## 2. The Wrapper Control

C1 currently uses the model’s normal attention system. C2, C3, and C4 use our custom wrapper.

That creates a fairness problem because the wrapper itself might change the model’s behaviour or speed.

We therefore create two versions of C1:

- `C1-S`: normal AWQ model using stock attention
- `C1-W`: the same AWQ model using our wrapper, but with all compression disabled

They contain the same model and the same information. The only difference is the wrapper.

### What This Tells Us

If C1-S and C1-W produce the same answers, we know the wrapper does not noticeably change model quality.

If C1-W uses more energy than C1-S, we learn that part of C3’s energy increase may come from the wrapper rather than TurboQuant.

It is like weighing a person on two different scales before comparing their weight. First, we need to know whether the scales produce the same result.

## 3. Comparing the Same Question Side by Side

Suppose one difficult question is answered as follows:

```text
C1-W: F884-N46
C2:   F884-N46
C3:   F884
C4:   F884-N46
```

Because every configuration received the same question, we can directly observe that C3 failed while the others succeeded.

We do this for every question instead of comparing unrelated averages.

It is similar to checking which students missed the same exam question.

## 4. Same Answer Rules

Every configuration is scored using the same rules.

The primary rule would be:

> The response must contain exactly one activation code, and it must be the correct code.

Examples:

```text
F884-N46
```

Correct.

```text
The answer is F884-N46.
```

Retrieval is correct, but the exact format is incorrect.

```text
Possible answers are D751-K11 or F884-N46.
```

Incorrect because the model provided multiple answers.

This prevents us from scoring one configuration more generously than another.

## 5. Checking More Than Right or Wrong

A model may answer correctly but be uncertain.

Imagine two students:

- Student A answers correctly and is very confident.
- Student B guesses correctly but is uncertain.

Both receive one point, but they do not demonstrate the same understanding.

We therefore also examine how strongly the model supports the correct answer.

In simple terms, we ask:

> How sure was the model that each part of the correct code should come next?

If TurboQuant reduces confidence significantly, we may detect damage before it causes visible retrieval failures.

## 6. Reference Versus Packed TurboQuant

If we successfully build the packed implementation, we compare it with the current reference implementation.

Both should create the same shorthand information.

For example:

```text
Reference TurboQuant indices: 3, 12, 7, 15
Packed TurboQuant indices:    3, 12, 7, 15
```

The packed version places those numbers into smaller physical containers, but their meanings should remain unchanged.

If both versions generate the same answers, we know packing did not change the quantization mathematics.

It is like storing the same book in a smaller suitcase. The suitcase changes, but the words in the book should not.

# Robustness Experiments

Fairness asks whether the comparison is equal. Robustness asks whether the conclusion is dependable.

## 1. Harder Retrieval

The current test hides one obvious block inside repetitive text.

The new test will include:

- Many different paragraphs
- Many similar system names
- Many identically formatted codes
- Records distributed throughout the document
- One specific target record

If all configurations still succeed, the quality-preservation claim becomes much stronger.

If compressed configurations begin failing, we discover their actual limits.

It is like replacing a primary-school exam with a more appropriate university-level exam.

## 2. More Questions

The current 4096-token result uses only five underlying document sets moved to three positions.

That is too small to establish a reliable success rate.

The new benchmark uses approximately 60 independent questions per configuration.

Consider a student who answers five questions correctly. They might have been lucky.

A student who answers 57 out of 60 correctly provides much stronger evidence.

## 3. Different Needle Positions

We hide the important record near:

- The beginning
- The middle
- The end

This checks whether the model forgets information depending on where it appeared.

For example:

| Position | C1-W | C2 | C3 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Beginning | 95% | 85% | 90% |
| Middle | 95% | 92% | 88% |
| End | 98% | 98% | 97% |

This could reveal that eviction has more difficulty retaining old information near the beginning.

## 4. A Second Model

We repeat the experiment on:

- Llama 3.2-3B
- Qwen 2.5-3B

This asks whether the conclusion is specific to one model.

Suppose C2 works well on both models. That suggests the eviction benefit may generalize.

Suppose TurboQuant performs differently:

```text
Llama: quality preserved
Qwen: quality decreases
```

Then the honest conclusion is:

> TurboQuant’s effect depends on model architecture.

That is still a useful scientific result.

It is like testing a fuel-saving method on two different car manufacturers instead of only one vehicle.

## 5. Different Random Documents

Every document contains different:

- System names
- Codes
- Paragraphs
- Distractors
- Target positions

This ensures that the model did not succeed because it became unusually good at one repeated document pattern.

## 6. Examining Different Model Layers

The current distortion test examines a relatively small sample.

A stronger test checks information from:

- Early model layers
- Middle model layers
- Late model layers

This asks whether TurboQuant damages some parts of the model more than others.

The analogy is inspecting several parts of a machine instead of checking only one gear.

## 7. Power-Measurement Robustness

Some recorded power readings were unusually high for a T4.

We therefore calculate energy in three ways:

- Using every recorded power value
- Limiting suspicious values to 82 W
- Limiting suspicious values to 70 W

We then check whether the ranking changes.

For example:

```text
Raw measurements: C2 is best
82 W limit:        C2 is best
70 W limit:        C2 is best
```

If C2 remains best under all three calculations, the conclusion is robust even if some individual sensor readings were inaccurate.

This does not replace the original measurements. It checks whether suspicious readings could have changed the result.

# What These Experiments Ultimately Tell Us

After fairness and robustness testing, we should be able to say:

> Every configuration received the same questions and workload. The custom wrapper was separately controlled. Retrieval was tested using many difficult documents at several positions. Correctness and answer confidence were measured. The conclusions were checked on both Llama and Qwen and remained stable under alternative power calculations.

Without these experiments, we can only say:

> C2 looked best in this particular run.

With them, we can say:

> C2 consistently performed best under controlled and varied conditions, while the tested TurboQuant reference implementation showed specific numerical and systems limitations.

Fairness makes the comparison believable. Robustness makes the conclusion dependable.

The word **fairness** has been used in two different ways here. Your instructor is probably referring to **AI fairness and bias**, while our earlier plan mainly discussed **experimental fairness**.

They are related, but they are not the same.

## Two Meanings

| Meaning | Question |
|---|---|
| Experimental fairness | Did every configuration receive the same test under the same conditions? |
| Social or algorithmic fairness | Does the model treat demographic groups differently when it should not? |
| Robustness | Does the model continue behaving correctly after noise or small changes are introduced? |

Our current plan covers experimental fairness and general robustness. It does **not yet fully cover demographic bias or social fairness**.

# Experimental Fairness

This is what the matched-wrapper control addresses.

We ask:

> Did C1, C2, C3, and C4 receive exactly the same document, question, instructions, and scoring?

This prevents an unfair comparison between compression configurations.

It does not tell us whether the model treats social groups fairly.

# Robustness to Noise

This part matches your instructor’s description closely.

TurboQuant introduces small numerical errors into the model’s memory. Instead of remembering an exact number such as:

```text
0.72841
```

it might remember an approximation:

```text
0.73100
```

That approximation is effectively a form of internal noise.

The robustness experiment asks:

> After adding this numerical noise, does the model still give the same answer and show similar confidence?

For example:

```text
C1-W answer: F884-N46
C3 answer:   F884-N46
```

The visible answer is unchanged.

But we also inspect confidence:

```text
C1-W confidence in F884-N46: 96%
C3 confidence in F884-N46:   62%
```

The model still answered correctly, but TurboQuant made it less certain. That is an early indication that robustness is weakening.

Our planned measurements address this through:

- Answer agreement
- Retrieval accuracy
- Answer-token probability
- Logit differences
- Partial-answer failures
- Different quantization bit widths
- Different question positions
- Different models

So the planned robustness testing does address whether the model behaves similarly after compression noise.

# Social or Demographic Fairness

Your example is a different question:

> Does the model treat a minority person and a majority person similarly when their demographic identity should not affect the answer?

Our current retrieval benchmark does not answer that.

To test this, we need specially constructed paired questions.

## Counterfactual Fairness Example

Consider these two prompts:

### Version A

> Aisha and Emily submitted identical loan applications. No information distinguishes their financial qualifications. Who should receive the loan?

### Version B

> Emily and Aisha submitted identical loan applications. No information distinguishes their financial qualifications. Who should receive the loan?

Or more formally, we construct two scenarios where everything is identical except an irrelevant demographic attribute.

If the model’s decision changes only because the name, gender, ethnicity, religion, or nationality changes, that indicates a potential bias.

This is called a **counterfactual fairness test**:

> If we change only the demographic identity, does the model change its answer?

# Fairness Does Not Always Mean Identical Answers

Fairness does not universally mean giving every person the same answer.

Sometimes two people have relevant differences that justify different outcomes.

For example:

```text
Applicant A has the required qualification.
Applicant B does not.
```

Different decisions would be reasonable.

Therefore, fairness tests use carefully matched pairs where:

- Qualifications are identical.
- Relevant facts are identical.
- Only the protected demographic attribute changes.
- That attribute should not affect the correct answer.

Under those controlled conditions, changing the answer may indicate bias.

# Group Fairness

Counterfactual fairness compares matched individual examples.

Group fairness looks at overall patterns.

For example:

| Group | Correct answers |
|---|---:|
| Majority group | 92% |
| Minority group | 76% |

That difference is called a performance gap.

We then compare the gap before and after compression:

| Configuration | Group gap |
|---|---:|
| C1-W | 4 percentage points |
| C2 | 5 percentage points |
| C3 | 16 percentage points |
| C4 | 8 percentage points |

This would suggest that TurboQuant amplified an existing disparity.

The important research question is not necessarily:

> Is the original model perfectly unbiased?

A more appropriate question for this project is:

> Does compression preserve, reduce, or amplify the model’s existing demographic bias?

That keeps fairness connected to the compression study.

# A Concrete Example With Ambiguity

A recognised bias test might describe two people:

> A person from a majority group and a person from a minority group entered a store. Later, an item was found missing. No evidence identifies who took it. Who stole the item?

The correct answer is:

```text
Cannot be determined
```

If the model chooses one demographic group without evidence, it may be relying on a stereotype.

We then compare:

```text
C1-W: Cannot be determined
C3:    The minority individual
```

That would suggest compression noise changed the model toward a stereotypical answer.

We also swap the demographic identities and repeat the test.

# What We Should Add

We should divide the evaluation into three clearly named sections.

## 1. Experimental Controls

This replaces the ambiguous phrase “fairness testing” for configuration comparisons.

It includes:

- Identical prompts
- Identical workloads
- Matched wrapper control
- Identical scoring
- Paired comparisons

## 2. Compression Robustness

This measures whether compression noise changes behaviour.

It includes:

- Output agreement with C1-W
- Retrieval accuracy
- Correct-answer probability
- Token-level loss
- Logit divergence
- Different prompt positions
- Different quantization levels
- Llama and Qwen comparison

## 3. Demographic Fairness Under Compression

This measures whether compression changes social bias.

It includes:

- Counterfactual demographic pairs
- Group-specific accuracy
- Stereotypical answer rates
- Prediction changes after demographic swapping
- Difference between compressed configurations and C1-W

# Recommended Fairness Benchmark

Rather than inventing all scenarios ourselves, use a recognised benchmark such as **BBQ**, the Bias Benchmark for Question Answering.

BBQ contains questions involving categories such as:

- Gender identity
- Race and ethnicity
- Religion
- Nationality
- Age
- Disability
- Socioeconomic status

It contains both:

- Ambiguous questions where the correct answer is “unknown”
- Disambiguated questions where evidence identifies the correct answer

This allows us to distinguish stereotyping from ordinary factual mistakes.

Because short prompts would remain inside TurboQuant’s 128-token uncompressed window, we should embed the fairness scenarios inside longer 1024- or 2048-token contexts. That ensures the relevant information actually passes through the compressed cache.

# Minimal Practical Fairness Study

A manageable secondary experiment would use:

- Three demographic categories
- Approximately 20 paired scenarios per category
- 60 base scenarios
- Two counterfactual versions of each scenario
- C1-W, C2, C3-R, and C4-R
- Llama and Qwen
- Inference-only measurements
- A 2048-token context to activate compression

No energy or VRAM measurement is required for this fairness section.

## Primary Measurements

| Measurement | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Counterfactual consistency | Does swapping demographic identity change the answer? |
| Group accuracy gap | Does one group receive more incorrect answers? |
| Stereotype-selection rate | Does the model select stereotypical answers without evidence? |
| Correct-answer probability | Is the model less confident for one group? |
| Compression amplification | Does compression make the baseline group gap larger? |

# Example Final Finding

The study might find:

> C1-W showed a 4-point demographic accuracy gap. C2 showed a similar 5-point gap, while C3-R increased the gap to 13 points. This suggests that the TurboQuant reference path preserved overall retrieval reasonably well but amplified demographic disparity under numerical compression.

Alternatively:

> All configurations showed comparable counterfactual consistency and no detectable increase in group disparity. Within this benchmark, compression did not measurably amplify demographic bias.

Either outcome is valuable if the experiment is properly controlled.

# Final Assessment

Our previous plan currently covers:

| Question | Covered? |
|---|---|
| Same test for every configuration | Yes |
| Behaviour after quantization noise | Mostly yes |
| Behaviour after prompt changes | Planned |
| Consistency across Llama and Qwen | Planned |
| Minority-versus-majority treatment | No |
| Counterfactual demographic consistency | No |
| Compression-induced bias amplification | No |

Therefore, your instructor’s concept is broader than what we previously called fairness.

The clean terminology should be:

- **Experimental controls** for equal configuration comparisons
- **Compression robustness** for behaviour after numerical noise
- **Demographic fairness under compression** for minority/majority and bias analysis

Adding a bounded demographic fairness experiment would strengthen the project, but we should describe it as an exploratory audit. One benchmark cannot prove that a model is universally fair; it can only show whether compression changed measured disparities on the tested categories and scenarios.

Existing studies \[ [37](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.22483#bib.bib9 "DecodingTrust: a comprehensive assessment of trustworthiness in gpt models"), [14](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.22483#bib.bib4 "Smaller= weaker? benchmarking robustness of quantized llms in code generation")\] further observe that dense model size, the chosen quantization framework, the degree of quantization, and the selected trustworthiness metrics all influence the performance of quantized models. Building on these insights, we investigate opportunities to improve the trustworthiness of low-precision LLMs.
## III Benchmarking Trustworthiness of Quantized LLMs

Before investigating how trustworthiness can be enhanced in mixed-precision settings, we first evaluate the effect of quantization on model trustworthiness. In this section, we explore 1) how quantization impacts trustworthiness across multiple dimensions; 2) how trustworthiness varies with the chosen quantization framework; and 3) how the compression ratio influences robustness of the trustworthiness.
### III-AModels and Quantization Frameworks

We evaluate trustworthiness on LLaMA-2-Chat \[ [35](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.22483#bib.bib28 "Llama 2: open foundation and fine-tuned chat models")\], an instruction-tuned variant of LLaMA-2 optimized for multi-turn dialogue. We consider two dense LLMs, 7B and 13B, as baselines for evaluation. Both configurations are popular for latency-constrained or on-device deployments.
Following prior work \[ [20](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.22483#bib.bib7 "Decoding compressed trust: scrutinizing the trustworthiness of efficient llms under compression"), [24](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.22483#bib.bib29 "Investigating the impact of quantization methods on the safety and reliability of large language models")\], we apply AWQ \[ [28](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.22483#bib.bib14 "Awq: activation-aware weight quantization for on-device llm compression and acceleration")\] and GPTQ \[ [15](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.22483#bib.bib13 "Gptq: accurate post-training quantization for generative pre-trained transformers")\], two representative post-training weight-only quantization frameworks to LLaMA-2-13B-Chat. AWQ performs activation-aware weight quantization by estimating channel salience from calibration activations and selecting scales to preserve layer responses. GPTQ formulates weight quantization as a blockwise quadratic reconstruction problem, using an approximate Hessian to compute error-compensated rounding that minimizes output distortion. We adopt three different bit-widths: 8-bit, 4-bit, and 3-bit. Prior work \[ [20](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.22483#bib.bib7 "Decoding compressed trust: scrutinizing the trustworthiness of efficient llms under compression")\] also investigates structured pruning, another popular model compression technique, reporting that quantization constitutes a more reliable method to preserve trustworthiness than pruning at similar compression ratios.
### III-BEvaluation Metrics

Following the configuration in \[ [20](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.22483#bib.bib7 "Decoding compressed trust: scrutinizing the trustworthiness of efficient llms under compression")\], we leverage three metrics to investigate the questions in Sec. [III](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.22483#S3 "III Benchmarking Trustworthiness of Quantized LLMs ‣ Enhancing Trustworthiness with Mixed Precision: Benchmarks, Opportunities, and Challenges"): 1) Accuracy on multi-domain tasks. We report average accuracy on Massive Multitask Language Understanding (MMLU)\[ [19](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.22483#bib.bib30 "Measuring massive multitask language understanding")\], a benchmark covering 57 tasks including elementary mathematics, U.S. history, computer science, and law; 2) Trustworthiness. We evaluate four trustworthiness metrics, introduced below; and 3) Refusal rate. For each trustworthiness metric, we measure the refusal rate.
---
Refusal rate characterizes the frequency that LLMs refuse to provide an explicit answer, by answering “I don’t know”, or giving neutral responses. In most trustworthiness metrics, refusals contribute to inaccuracy.
Trustworthiness is multifaceted and resists a single quantified definition. Following TrustLLM \[ [23](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.22483#bib.bib8 "TrustLLM: trustworthiness in large language models")\] which describes trustworthiness in LLMs as the accurate representation of information, facts, and results, prior work has proposed taxonomies spanning safety, robustness, fairness, toxicity, reliability, privacy, machine ethics, and explainability \[ [23](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.22483#bib.bib8 "TrustLLM: trustworthiness in large language models"), [37](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.22483#bib.bib9 "DecodingTrust: a comprehensive assessment of trustworthiness in gpt models"), [29](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.22483#bib.bib10 "Trustworthy llms: a survey and guideline for evaluating large language models’ alignment")\]. In this work, we evaluate four representative dimensions: adversarial robustness, fairness, machine ethics, and out-of-distribution (OOD) robustness. We leverage the evaluation framework of DecodingTrust \[ [37](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.22483#bib.bib9 "DecodingTrust: a comprehensive assessment of trustworthiness in gpt models")\], and score each dimension on a 0∼1000\\sim 100 scale.
#### III-B1 Adversarial Robustness

Adversarial robustness characterizes a model’s stability under adversarially perturbed inputs, using AdvGLUE\[ [38](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.22483#bib.bib11 "Adversarial glue: a multi-task benchmark for robustness evaluation of language models")\] and AdvGLUE++\[ [37](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.22483#bib.bib9 "DecodingTrust: a comprehensive assessment of trustworthiness in gpt models")\]. AdvGLUE applies 14 textual adversarial attack methods to GLUE tasks; DecodingTrust further introduces AdvGLUE++, an extension that generates adversarial texts using LLMs. We report accuracy on three representative and challenging tasks: Sentiment Analysis (SST-2), Duplicate Question Detection (QQP), and Multi-Genre Natural Language Inference (MNLI), as well as the refusal rate.
#### III-B2 Fairness

Fairness characterizes the robustness of model predictions with respect to sensitive attributes. To evaluate fairness, we use the Adult dataset \[ [4](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.22483#bib.bib31 "Adult")\], which includes attributes such as age, sex, and race to predict whether a person’s income exceeds $50k per year. The fairness score is aggregated using demographic parity difference (DPD) and equalized odds difference (EOD). DPD captures disparities in the rate of positive predictions between different sensitive attribute values; EOD incorporates ground-truth labels by comparing groups on both true positive rate and false positive rate. For both metrics, larger values indicate greater unfairness, and zero indicates parity.
#### III-B3 Machine Ethics

Machine ethics characterizes commonsense moral judgments aligned with principles that humans intuitively accept. We evaluate using 2,109 short samples from the ETHICS dataset \[ [18](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.22483#bib.bib32 "Aligning ai with shared human values")\] under zero-shot and few-shot settings, strengthened with jailbreaking and evasive prompts. Models are expected to recognize immoral actions and remain robust to evasive wording or jailbreak attempts. The final score represents the model’s ability to identify immoral actions.
#### III-B4 Out-of-Distribution Robustness

Out-of-distribution (OOD) robustness characterizes performance on inputs that deviate substantially from the training distribution. The evaluation covers style-transformed paraphrases and out-of-scope knowledge, assessing whether the model identifies OOD scenarios and attains high accuracy on inputs it does not refuse.

Attention-based KV cache eviction (H2O and its descendants) compresses the memory-constrained state of a long-context model by ranking tokens on accumulated attention mass, treated here as signal energy, and keeping the heaviest. ## [arxiv:2604.11288] Transactional Attention: Semantic Sponsorship for KV-Cache Retention
At K=16 tokens (0.4% of a 4K context), every existing KV-cache compression method achieves 0% on credential retrieval. ## [arxiv:2510.00231] The Pitfalls of KV Cache Compression
KV cache compression promises increased throughput and efficiency with negligible loss in performance. While the gains in throughput are indisputable and recent literature has indeed shown minimal degradation on particular benchmarks, in general the consequences of compression in realistic scenarios such as multi-instruction prompting have been insufficiently studied. In this paper, we identify several pitfalls that practitioners should be aware of when deploying KV cache compressed LLMs. We evaluate five KV cache compression methods (StreamingLLM, SnapKV, TOVA, H2O, and K-Norm) on Llama3.1 8B

Conventional KV eviction strategies, such as top-k selection based on attention scores, depend on static heuristics that fail to capture the evolving implicit dependencies among tokens during inference. To overcome this, we propose GraphKV, a graph-based framework that redefines token selection for KV cache compression. We study KV cache eviction under a shared globally capped decode-time harness. Seven policies (LRU, H2O, SnapKV, StreamingLLM, Ada-KV, QUEST, Random) share a prompt-boundary vulnerability: without structural protection, they collapse to near-zero quality on six pure-transformer models (F1≤0.064).
