# The Impact of Inference Acceleration on Bias of LLMs

Elisabeth Kirsten1,3, Ivan Habernal1,3, Vedant Nanda2, Muhammad Bilal Zafar1,3  
1Ruhr University Bochum, 2Aleph Alpha,  
3UAR Research Center for Trustworthy Data Science and Security  
Correspondence: [elisabeth.kirsten@rub.de](mailto:elisabeth.kirsten@rub.de)

###### Abstract

Last few years have seen unprecedented advances in capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs). These advancements promise to benefit a vast array of application domains. However, due to their immense size, performing inference with LLMs is both costly and slow. Consequently, a plethora of recent work has proposed strategies to enhance inference efficiency, *e.g.*, quantization, pruning, and caching. These acceleration strategies reduce the inference cost and latency, often by several factors, while maintaining much of the predictive performance measured via common benchmarks. In this work, we explore another critical aspect of LLM performance: demographic bias in model generations due to inference acceleration optimizations. Using a wide range of metrics, we probe bias in model outputs from a number of angles. Analysis of outputs before and after inference acceleration shows significant change in bias. Worryingly, these bias effects are complex and unpredictable. A combination of an acceleration strategy and bias type may show little bias change in one model but may lead to a large effect in another. Our results highlight a need for in-depth and case-by-case evaluation of model bias after it has been modified to accelerate inference.

This paper contains prompts and outputs which may be deemed offensive.

The Impact of Inference Acceleration on Bias of LLMs

  

Elisabeth Kirsten1,3, Ivan Habernal1,3, Vedant Nanda2, Muhammad Bilal Zafar1,3 1Ruhr University Bochum, 2Aleph Alpha, 3UAR Research Center for Trustworthy Data Science and Security Correspondence: [elisabeth.kirsten@rub.de](mailto:elisabeth.kirsten@rub.de)

  

## 1 Introduction

Modern-day LLMs like LLaMA and GPT-4 show remarkable language generation capabilities, leading to a surge in their popularity and adoption (Ziems et al., [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.22118v3#bib.bib49); Wei et al., [2022](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.22118v3#bib.bib46); Bubeck et al., [2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.22118v3#bib.bib8)). However, owing to their immense size, deploying these models can be challenging, or even infeasible for consumer-grade devices. A flurry of research has proposed acceleration strategies such as quantization and pruning to enable efficient inference (Park et al., [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.22118v3#bib.bib35); Zhu et al., [2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.22118v3#bib.bib48)). The objective of these strategies is typically to reduce the model size while maintaining predictive performance. Over time, these strategies have become increasingly prevalent with integration into popular libraries like HuggingFace (Hug, [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.22118v3#bib.bib2)) and vLLM (Kwon et al., [2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.22118v3#bib.bib26)).

While these inference acceleration strategies aim to preserve predictive performance, they may inadvertently lead to some side-effects (Jaiswal et al., [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.22118v3#bib.bib24); Gonçalves and Strubell, [2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.22118v3#bib.bib19)). For example, compression techniques might significantly reduce model trustworthiness (Hong et al., [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.22118v3#bib.bib21)). On the other hand, smaller models have been found to mitigate privacy risks and reduce egocentric tendencies in the generated text (Perez et al., [2022](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.22118v3#bib.bib36); Sun et al., [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.22118v3#bib.bib40); Hong et al., [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.22118v3#bib.bib21)).

In this paper, we explore how demographic bias in the model output changes after the implementation of inference acceleration strategies. Specifically, we aim to answer the following questions:

RQ1

Are certain bias types more prone to manifesting because of inference acceleration?

RQ2

Are certain inference acceleration strategies more prone to bias?

RQ3

Does the bias impact of a strategy remain consistent across various models?

Prompt

You will be shown a list of individuals, a decision-making scenario, and a question about which individual is the most suitable candidate for this scenario. Your task is to identify the individual. The individuals are: a man, a woman, a non-binary person.  
The scenario is: The backstage pass applicant is a student interested in attending local music festivals. They have been volunteering at the festival’s information booth for a few years and would like to get a backstage pass \[...\].  
The question is: Which individual should the festival organizers grant the backstage pass?

Base

The answer is: The individual who is known for being friendly, hard-working and responsible, regardless of their gender.

Quantized

The answer is: The non-binary person. This individual has a positive track record of being friendly, hard-working and responsible. \[...\]

Table 1: \[Mistral-7B model on DiscrimEvalGen data\] Decisions made by the base model and its 4-bit weight quantized version. The choice and reasoning changes from the base to the quantized version.

Our assessment includes five commonly used inference acceleration techniques and three widely used LLMs. Noting the multidimensional nature of bias (Mehrabi et al., [2022](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.22118v3#bib.bib31)), we test the models with six different bias metrics. Our results show that inference acceleration strategies can have significant impacts on bias. [Table 1](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.22118v3#S1.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ The Impact of Inference Acceleration on Bias of LLMs") provides an example of the effects of acceleration using 4-bit AWQ Quantization (Lin et al., [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.22118v3#bib.bib28)) on a model’s decision. Some acceleration strategies are more prone to bias than others. For instance, whereas AWQ Quantization leads to a significant change in bias for some model/bias metric combinations, KV-cache quantization mostly remains robust. The effect of inference acceleration on bias can be unpredictable with the change in magnitude and direction of bias often varying across models. For example, AWQ quantization did not negatively impact LLaMA-2 or LLaMA-3.1 models’ agreeability with stereotypes, but significantly increased stereotyping behavior for Mistral-0.3.

Overall, our results show a need for careful evaluations when applying inference acceleration, as the downstream impact on bias can be unpredictable and significant in magnitude.

The code for our experiments is available at [https://github.com/aisoc-lab/inference-acceleration-bias](https://github.com/aisoc-lab/inference-acceleration-bias).

## 2 Related Work

Most evaluations of inference acceleration strategies focus on application-agnostic metrics like perplexity or predictive performance-driven tasks like MMLU (Lin et al., [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.22118v3#bib.bib28); Sun et al., [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.22118v3#bib.bib40); Dettmers et al., [2022](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.22118v3#bib.bib12); Hooper et al., [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.22118v3#bib.bib22)). However, recent work has shown that model compression can result in degradation of model performance in areas beyond predictive performance (Jaiswal et al., [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.22118v3#bib.bib24); Gonçalves and Strubell, [2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.22118v3#bib.bib19)).

The effect of model size on trust criteria. Recent work has started exploring the impact of model size on trust related criteria. For example, Perez et al. ([2022](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.22118v3#bib.bib36)) find that larger models tend to overly agree with user views. Sun et al. ([2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.22118v3#bib.bib40)) show that smaller models can reduce privacy risks. Huang et al. ([2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.22118v3#bib.bib23)) find that smaller models are more vulnerable to backdoor attacks. Mo et al. ([2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.22118v3#bib.bib32)) find that larger models are more susceptible to manipulation through malicious demonstrations. Jaiswal et al. ([2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.22118v3#bib.bib24)) offer a fine-grained benchmark for evaluating the performance of compressed LLMs on more intricate, knowledge-intensive tasks such as reasoning, summarization, and in-context retrieval. By measuring perplexity, they show that pruned models suffer from performance degradation, whereas quantized models tend to perform better. Xu and Hu ([2022](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.22118v3#bib.bib47)) find that knowledge distillation causes a monotonic reduction in toxicity in GPT-2, though it shows only small improvements in reducing bias on counterfactual embedding-based datasets. These analyses differ from our paper in one of the following ways: (i) they are limited to less recent, pre-trained models, which may not adequately represent the complexities of modern LLMs with significantly more parameters; (ii) they target trustworthiness desiderata beyond bias, *e.g.*, backdoor attacks.

Effect of inference acceleration on trustworthiness. Gonçalves and Strubell ([2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.22118v3#bib.bib19)) measure the impact of quantization and knowledge distillation on LLMs, and show that longer pretraining and larger models correlate with higher demographic bias, while quantization appears to have a regularizing effect. The bias metrics they consider focus on embeddings or token output probabilities, while we consider a larger range of metrics that focus on properties of generated texts. Hong et al. ([2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.22118v3#bib.bib21)), in a follow-up to Wang et al. ([2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.22118v3#bib.bib45)), provide a broader assessment of trustworthiness under compression strategies like quantization and pruning, including adversarial settings. However, their study relies on a single metric to evaluate stereotype bias, which may not capture the broader complexity of bias. We, on the other hand, aim to provide a comprehensive evaluation of bias across multiple dimensions to better understand the impact of inference acceleration strategies. Finally, while these previous benchmarks show largely uniform and predictable effects of inference acceleration on bias, by leveraging a richer set of metrics, our analysis shows a much more nuanced picture and a need for case-by-case evaluation.

## 3 Measuring Bias in LLM Outputs

ML bias can stem from different causes (Suresh and Guttag, [2021](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.22118v3#bib.bib41)), can manifest in various manners (Blodgett et al., [2020](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.22118v3#bib.bib7); Mehrabi et al., [2022](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.22118v3#bib.bib31)), and can cause different types of harms (Gallegos et al., [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.22118v3#bib.bib18)). While a detailed examination can be found in Gallegos et al. ([2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.22118v3#bib.bib18)), bias in LLMs is often categorized into the following meta-groups:

1.  1.
    
    Embedding-based metrics use representations of words or phrases from different demographic groups, *e.g.*, WEAT (Caliskan et al., [2017](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.22118v3#bib.bib9)) and SEAT (May et al., [2019](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.22118v3#bib.bib30)).
    
2.  2.
    
    Probability-based metrics compare the probabilities assigned by the model to different demographic groups, *e.g.*, CrowSPairs (Nangia et al., [2020](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.22118v3#bib.bib34)).
    
3.  3.
    
    Generated text-based metrics analyze model generations and compute differences across demographics, *e.g.*, by evaluating model responses to standardized questionnaires (Durmus et al., [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.22118v3#bib.bib15)), or using classifiers to analyze the characteristics of generations such as toxicity (Hartvigsen et al., [2022](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.22118v3#bib.bib20); Smith et al., [2022](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.22118v3#bib.bib39); Dhamala et al., [2021](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.22118v3#bib.bib13)).
    

We leave out embedding-based metrics from our analysis since (i) the more typical use-case of modern, instruction-tuned LLMs like LLaMA and GPT-4 is prompt-tuning or fine-tuning rather than adapting the models using embeddings and (ii) embedding bias is not guaranteed to lead to bias in the text generations. While we initially considered classification-based bias metrics (*e.g.*, those in [Dhamala et al.](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.22118v3#bib.bib13)) which consider difference in measures like toxicity and sentiment on common datasets like Wikipedia. A preliminary analysis showed very little overall toxicity in model outputs, most likely due to heavy alignment on these datasets. For this reason, we did not further consider these metrics.

With these considerations in mind, the final set of metrics we consider is as follows. We add further information, *e.g.*, the number of inputs and license types, in [Appendix A](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.22118v3#A1 "Appendix A Additional Reproducibility Details ‣ The Impact of Inference Acceleration on Bias of LLMs").

CrowSPairs (Nangia et al., [2020](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.22118v3#bib.bib34)) is a dataset of crowd-sourced sentence pairs designed to evaluate stereotypes related to race, gender, sexual orientation, religion, age, nationality, disability, physical appearance, and socioeconomic status. Each pair consists of one sentence that demonstrates a stereotype and the other that demonstrates the opposite of the stereotype. GlobalOpinionQA (Durmus et al., [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.22118v3#bib.bib15)) uses multiple-choice questions to assess the opinions stated by a model relative to aggregated population opinions from different countries. The goal is to identify model bias in representing diverse viewpoints. We follow the same measurement procedure as [Durmus et al.](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.22118v3#bib.bib15) with one exception: we use the Wasserstein distance as our divergence metric. [Durmus et al.](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.22118v3#bib.bib15) use 1-Jensen-Shannon distance, which can become highly skewed when the distributions have very little or no overlap. In contrast, the Wasserstein distance is more sensitive to the geometry of the probability distributions Arjovsky et al. ([2017](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.22118v3#bib.bib5)). We compute the Wasserstein distance using the implementation provided by the Python scipy library (Virtanen et al., [2020](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.22118v3#bib.bib44)).

The final bias value is then the Gini coefficient of the Wasserstein distance for each country. The metric lies in the range \[0,1\]01\[0,1\]\[ 0 , 1 \]. The dataset does not provide responses from all countries to all questions, making it difficult to analyze overall value tendencies consistently. To address this, we exclude countries that do not have responses to at least 50 questions from our analysis.

WorldBench (Moayeri et al., [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.22118v3#bib.bib33)) evaluates performance disparities in an LLM’s ability to recall facts (*e.g.*, population, GDP, and capital) about different countries. Moayeri et al. ([2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.22118v3#bib.bib33)) structure the questions to elicit a single numerical answer. The dataset encompasses 11111111 statistics for about 200200200200 countries. To compare numerical answers, we calculate the absolute relative error between the model’s answer and the ground truth, and average the error over all questions to obtain a single score per model. This score lies in the range \[0,1\]01\[0,1\]\[ 0 , 1 \].

DT–Stereotyping. DecodingTrust (Wang et al., [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.22118v3#bib.bib45)) is a framework for evaluating the trustworthiness of LLMs across eight dimensions, one of which is stereotype bias. The dataset consists of custom-made statements (from now on referred to as DT-Stereotyping) designed to provoke unsafe (*e.g.*, biased, toxic) responses. Following Wang et al. ([2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.22118v3#bib.bib45)), we ask the model to either agree or disagree with these statements. DiscrimEvalGen. The original design of DiscrimEval evaluates bias by analyzing the probability of the first token being “yes” or “no”, reducing the model’s output to a simplified binary decision. This approach has the following limitations:

1.  1.
    
    It only considers the first output token, ignoring the rest of the generation.
    
2.  2.
    
    Even at the first token, the bias is computed by considering the Softmax probabilities of ‘yes’ and ‘no’ which could be miscalibrated and may not adequately capture the model’s uncertainty  (Cruz et al., [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.22118v3#bib.bib11)).
    
3.  3.
    
    The model is required to independently evaluate each person and could potentially assign advantageous outcomes to everyone regardless of their demographic features. Such an unconstrained setup may not test more subtle inclinations of the model, *e.g.*, preferences when required to make a choice between different demographic groups or refusing to make a choice at all. In fact, Bai et al. ([2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.22118v3#bib.bib6)) show that GPT-4 assigns benefits to various demographic groups in similar proportions.
    

With the aim of overcoming these issues, we propose a new dataset DiscrimEvalGen. While DiscrimEval asks the same question separately for each demographic group g𝑔gitalic\_g, DiscrimEvalGen forces the model to make a single choice. Specifically, we (i) present the question to the model and describe that the candidates are persons from different groups, *e.g.*, a man, a woman, a non-binary person; (ii) describe that the benefit (*e.g.*, a work contract) can be granted to only a single person; and (iii) ask the model to make its choice.

[Figure A.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.22118v3#A1.F1 "Figure A.1 ‣ Appendix A Additional Reproducibility Details ‣ The Impact of Inference Acceleration on Bias of LLMs") in [Appendix A](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.22118v3#A1 "Appendix A Additional Reproducibility Details ‣ The Impact of Inference Acceleration on Bias of LLMs") shows a concrete example. To avoid having a very long list of choices (135135135135 intersectional groups in the original dataset), we limit the groups to those based on gender, that is, G\={man,non-binary,woman}𝐺mannon-binarywomanG=\\{\\text{man},\\text{non-binary},\\text{woman}\\}italic\_G = { man , non-binary , woman }. We encountered several cases where the model refuses to select a single person, or selects several persons. We ignore such cases from the bias computation. If for a particular model/acceleration strategy combination, we have more than 80%percent8080\\%80 % such cases, we drop this combination from our results.

Just like DT-Stereotyping, we consider two versions: DiscrimEvalGen (greedy) with T\=0𝑇0T=0italic\_T = 0 and DiscrimEvalGen (sampling) with T\=1𝑇1T=1italic\_T = 1 and top-p\=1top-p1\\text{top-p}=1top-p = 1.

## 4 Experimental Setup

Models and Infrastructure. We analyze three different models: LLaMA-2 (Touvron et al., [2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.22118v3#bib.bib43)), LLaMA-3.1 (Dubey et al., [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.22118v3#bib.bib14)), and Mistral-0.3 (Jiang et al., [2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.22118v3#bib.bib25)). We consider the smallest size variant of each model: LLaMA-2-7B, LLaMA-3.1-8B, and Mistral-7B-v0.3 (license information in Appendix [A](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.22118v3#A1 "Appendix A Additional Reproducibility Details ‣ The Impact of Inference Acceleration on Bias of LLMs")). These models were selected due to their recency, widespread use, and compatibility with our resource constraints, which included a single node equipped with four NVIDIA A100 GPUs that was shared among several research teams. Our evaluation focuses on the chat versions of these models, which are specifically designed to align with human values and preferences. We used the GitHub Copilot IDE plugin to assist with coding.

Inference acceleration strategies. We consider inference time acceleration techniques that do not require re-training. This choice allows us to evaluate models in a real-world scenario where users download pre-trained models and apply them to their tasks without further data- or compute-intensive modifications. We focus on strategies that aim to speed up inference by approximating the outputs of the base model, and where the approximations results in measurable changes in the model output. This criterion excludes strategies like speculative decoding (Leviathan et al., [2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.22118v3#bib.bib27)) where the output of the base and inference accelerated models are often the same. Specifically, we consider the following strategies:

Quantization. We consider the following variants:

1.  1.
    
    INT4 or INT8 quantization using Bitsandbytes library (Bit, [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.22118v3#bib.bib1)) which first normalizes the model weights to store common values efficiently. Then, it quantizes the weights to 4 or 8 bits for storage. Depending on the implementation, the weights are either dequantized to fp16 during inference or custom kernels perform low-bit matrix multiplications while still efficiently utilizing tensor cores for matrix multiplications.
    
2.  2.
    
    Activation-aware Weight Quantization (AWQ) (Lin et al., [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.22118v3#bib.bib28)) quantizes the parameters by taking into account the data distribution in the activations produced by the model during inference. We use the 4-bit version as the authors do not provide an 8-bit implementation.
    
3.  3.
    
    Key-Value Cache Quantization (KV4 or KV8) dynamically compresses the KV cache during inference. KV cache is a key component of fast LLM inference and can take significant space on the GPU. Thus, quantizing the cache can allow using larger KV caches for even faster inference. We use both 4 and 8-bit quantization (Liu et al., [2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.22118v3#bib.bib29)). We use the native HuggingFace implementation. This implementation does not support Mistral models.
    

Pruning removes a subset of model weights to reduce the high computational cost of LLMs while aiming to preserve performance. Traditional pruning methods require retraining (Cheng et al., [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.22118v3#bib.bib10)). More recent approaches prune weights post-training in iterative weight-update processes, *e.g.*, SparseGPT (Frantar and Alistarh, [2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.22118v3#bib.bib17)). We use the Wanda method by Sun et al. ([2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.22118v3#bib.bib40)) which uses a pruning metric based on both weight magnitudes and input activation norms. The sparse model obtained after pruning is directly usable without further fine-tuning. We consider two variants: (i) Unstructured Pruning (WU) with a sparsity ratio of 50%percent5050\\%50 %, eliminating 50%percent5050\\%50 % of the weights connected to each output; and (ii) Structured Pruning (WS) which induces a structured N:M sparsity, where at most N out of every M contiguous weights are allowed to be non-zero, allowing the computation to leverage matrix-based GPU optimizations. We use a 2:4:242:42 : 4 compression rate. Prior work has shown that pruned models can preserve comparable performance levels even at high compression rates (Sun et al., [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.22118v3#bib.bib40); Jaiswal et al., [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.22118v3#bib.bib24); Frantar and Alistarh, [2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.22118v3#bib.bib17)), *e.g.*, 2:4:242:42 : 4 considered here.

Parameters. As described in Section [3](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.22118v3#S3 "3 Measuring Bias in LLM Outputs ‣ The Impact of Inference Acceleration on Bias of LLMs"), most bias metrics are designed such that they only support greedy decoding, resulting in deterministic outputs. Only DT-Stereotyping and DiscrimEvalGen support stochastic decoding in addition to greedy decoding. When using stochastic decoding, we sample the output 5555 times and report the average bias.

The models can be used with and without the developer-prescribed instruction templates (with special tokens specifying the start and end of instructions). Past investigations have shown that instruction and answer formats can have an unpredictable impact on the model performance (Fourrier et al., [2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.22118v3#bib.bib16); Alzahrani et al., [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.22118v3#bib.bib4)). However, the impact of using or not using the instruction template on model bias is less well understood. We thus study both configurations. The main paper includes the results without the template, while results with instructions templates are shown in [Appendix C](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.22118v3#A3 "Appendix C Results With Instruction / Chat Template ‣ The Impact of Inference Acceleration on Bias of LLMs").

Acceleration strategies can have significant, though sometimes subtle, impacts on bias in LLMs. The effect on bias varies depending on the dataset, model, and scenario used.

## 5 Results

[Table 2](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.22118v3#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4 Experimental Setup ‣ The Impact of Inference Acceleration on Bias of LLMs") shows the bias of base models w.r.t. each metric, and the change in bias as a result of inference acceleration. We show examples of generations and further output characteristics in the Appendix. The table shows that inference acceleration strategies can have significant, albeit nuanced, impacts on bias in LLMs. While some strategies consistently reduce certain biases, others yield mixed results depending on the model and context. The results also show that while the input probability-based metric, CrowSPairs, does not show much change in bias across the board, considering a wider range of metrics paints a much more diverse picture. While the exact magnitude of changes varies, we largely see similar trends of unpredictable effects on downstream bias both with and without the instruction template (Appendix [C](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.22118v3#A3 "Appendix C Results With Instruction / Chat Template ‣ The Impact of Inference Acceleration on Bias of LLMs")). Although we did not track the exact runtime, our experiments required several GPU days to complete. We now analyze each RQ from Section [1](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.22118v3#S1 "1 Introduction ‣ The Impact of Inference Acceleration on Bias of LLMs") in detail.

### RQ1: Are certain bias types more prone to manifesting because of inference acceleration?

Inference acceleration strategies have disparate impacts on different types of bias metrics. Specifically, we see:

No significant impact on log-likelihood of stereotypical sentences as measured by the CrowsPairs dataset. Most acceleration strategies show little to no significant effect on the log-likelihood of counterfactual sentences. The results are largely in line with Gonçalves and Strubell ([2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.22118v3#bib.bib19)) who also show a relatively mild effect of quantization on bias measured via CrowSPairs, although they consider the previous generation of LMs like BERT and RoBERTa. We provide a detailed breakdown of results per bias type in [Table B.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.22118v3#A2.T1 "Table B.1 ‣ Analysis of Text Characteristics ‣ Appendix B Additional Results ‣ The Impact of Inference Acceleration on Bias of LLMs"). Structured pruning leads to small improvements in bias scores for certain bias types, such as "age". However, the average improvements over the base model across all bias types are modest, generally less than 10%.

Subtle shifts in values and opinions in the GlobalOpinionQA task. We observe little effect of inference strategies on the values and opinions represented by the models (see [2(b)](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.22118v3#S4.T2.st2 "2(b) ‣ Table 2 ‣ 4 Experimental Setup ‣ The Impact of Inference Acceleration on Bias of LLMs")). AWQ quantization increased bias across all models, with changes of up to 36%. Structured pruning also leads to noticeable shifts, including a 45% increase in bias scores for Mistral. Despite these changes, overall bias scores remain low, suggesting that the general similarity of responses across countries is largely unaffected. Notably, KV cache quantization shows no negative impact. While the overall similarity of responses per country often remains stable, there are still subtle shifts in the ranking of individual countries, as reflected in the world maps in [Figure B.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.22118v3#A2.F1 "Figure B.1 ‣ Analysis of Text Characteristics ‣ Appendix B Additional Results ‣ The Impact of Inference Acceleration on Bias of LLMs").

Pruning influences models’ ability to recall country-specific facts. In the WorldBench dataset, 8-bit and KV cache quantization showed improvements in mean average error, whereas pruning strategies and AWQ quantization increased bias scores. We report detailed disparity scores across income groups and regions in [Table B.5](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.22118v3#A2.T5 "Table B.5 ‣ Analysis of Text Characteristics ‣ Appendix B Additional Results ‣ The Impact of Inference Acceleration on Bias of LLMs"). Pruning leads to higher disparities across regions and income groups in 8/12 cases. In contrast, other inference acceleration methods had non-uniform or minimal influence on models’ factual recall performance across countries.

More pronounced shifts in model’s agreement with stereotypes. The DT-Stereotyping task reveals significant changes in agreement, disagreement, and no-response rates across strategies. Pruning strategies tend to reduce disagreement with stereotypes, leading to higher agreement or no-response rates ([Table B.2](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.22118v3#A2.T2a "Table B.2 ‣ Analysis of Text Characteristics ‣ Appendix B Additional Results ‣ The Impact of Inference Acceleration on Bias of LLMs")). Quantization showed minimal effects or slight improvements for LLaMA models but increased the number of agreements with stereotypes for Mistral. In general, inference acceleration significantly changes models’ agreement with stereotypes.

Varying bias patterns in allocation-based decision-making scenarios. In DiscrimEval, structured pruning consistently achieved the lowest bias score across models, followed closely by KV cache quantization. On the other hand, AWQ quantization resulted in a notable increase in bias.

In the DiscrimEvalGen dataset, which measures bias in relative decision making scenarios and longer text generations, we observe more significant shifts in resource allocation based on gender, with AWQ leading to increased bias across models and sampling strategies. A detailed breakdown of decisions per model and tested attributes in [Table B.4](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.22118v3#A2.T4 "Table B.4 ‣ Analysis of Text Characteristics ‣ Appendix B Additional Results ‣ The Impact of Inference Acceleration on Bias of LLMs") shows that inference acceleration strategies influence the models’ tendency to give no response or refuse an answer. Both Mistral and LLaMA-3.1 display a tendency to favor the non-binary person, though this effect is reduced when pruning strategies are applied.

### RQ2: Are certain inference acceleration strategies more prone to bias?

[Table 2](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.22118v3#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4 Experimental Setup ‣ The Impact of Inference Acceleration on Bias of LLMs") shows that the change in bias heavily depends on the acceleration strategy. Notably, AWQ quantization performed worse than suggested by recent work (Hong et al., [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.22118v3#bib.bib21)), leading to massively increased bias in DiscrimEval scenarios for LLaMA-2 and Mistral, and heightened agreement with stereotypical statements in DT-Stereotyping for Mistral. While previous work by [Hong et al.](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.22118v3#bib.bib21) suggested that quantization is an effective compression technique with minimal impact on trustworthiness, our findings highlight the need to evaluate these strategies across multiple models and evaluation contexts to capture their broader effects.

KV cache quantization and structured Wanda pruning showed promising trends across datasets and models, frequently showing minimal changes or slight improvements in bias scores. However, structured pruning exhibited certain drawbacks. When examining parse rates and no-response rates, we found that this strategy can cause the model to fail to perform the task, follow instructions, or produce nonsensical, repetitive outputs. Overall, our results suggest quantizing weights can have more drastic, unpredictable impacts on bias compared to KV cache quantization.

### RQ3: Does the bias impact of a strategy remain consistent across models?

The effects of inference acceleration strategies on stereotype agreeability vary markedly across models. A detailed breakdown of agreement, disagreement, and no-response rates for nucleus sampling in [Table B.2](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.22118v3#A2.T2a "Table B.2 ‣ Analysis of Text Characteristics ‣ Appendix B Additional Results ‣ The Impact of Inference Acceleration on Bias of LLMs") illustrates how the models’ baselines already differ. LLaMA models most frequently provide no response, while Mistral shows a higher rate of both agreement and disagreement. Notably, the impact of inference acceleration strategies is much more pronounced for Mistral, with agreements increasing by over 75%percent7575\\%75 % relative to the base model for both AWQ and unstructured pruning.

Additionally, different models display varying abilities to follow instructions and perform tasks. For example, in the DiscrimEvalGen dataset ([Table B.4](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.22118v3#A2.T4 "Table B.4 ‣ Analysis of Text Characteristics ‣ Appendix B Additional Results ‣ The Impact of Inference Acceleration on Bias of LLMs")), LLaMA-2 mostly provides no response. Mistral tends to give answers more frequently in its base form but shows a reduced tendency to respond under quantization and even more so under pruning strategies.

Our findings demonstrate that the impact of a single acceleration strategy does not remain consistent across different models. The baseline performance of each model often shows divergent trends, and these disparities are further amplified by inference acceleration strategies. This highlights the need for a model-by-model evaluation when assessing a strategy’s impact on bias.

Comparing 4-bit and 8-bit compression. While lower-bit compression can enhance efficiency, it often risks degrading model performance (Hong et al., [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.22118v3#bib.bib21)). Hong et al. ([2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.22118v3#bib.bib21)) explored compression down to 3-bit quantized models, highlighting 4-bit as a setting that balances efficiency and fairness. In our experiments, we evaluate both 4-bit and 8-bit quantization for weights and KV-cache. For 8-bit weight quantization, bias scores generally remain close to those of the base models, with small improvements observed in some cases, except for a slight increase in bias on the DiscrimEval dataset. Similarly, 4-bit weight quantization yields comparable results, though it leads to noticeable increases in bias scores for DT-Stereotyping and DiscrimEvalGen, particularly for the Mistral model. KV-cache quantization consistently shows minimal impact on bias across datasets, with 8-bit compression having little to no noticeable effect on bias, while 4-bit demonstrates small improvements in some model/dataset combinations.

Combining inference acceleration strategies. We also explore the impact of multiple inference acceleration strategies on model bias. In Table [3](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.22118v3#S5.T3 "Table 3 ‣ RQ3: Does the bias impact of a strategy remain consistent across models? ‣ 5 Results ‣ The Impact of Inference Acceleration on Bias of LLMs"), we compare INT4 quantization, 4-bit KV cache quantization, and a combination of both. We observe that the outcomes of the combined strategies differ from applying them individually. In some cases, the bias observed aligns with INT4 quantization (*e.g.*, for DiscrimEval), in others with KV cache quantization (*e.g.*, for DiscrimEvalGen). This result further underscores our finding that the effects of inference acceleration strategies on bias are complex and often unpredictable.

Effects of using provider-prescribed instruction templates. We study whether using provider-prescribed instruction templates ameliorates the bias resulting from inference acceleration. A small AI-fairness experiment would strengthen responsible evaluation, but it would add **limited novelty by itself** and could distract from the project’s main contribution.

## Existing Research

This topic is no longer unexplored.

Most importantly, *The Impact of Inference Acceleration on Bias of LLMs* (`arXiv:2410.22118`) already evaluated:

- AWQ and other weight quantization
- 4-bit and 8-bit KV-cache quantization
- Combined weight and KV quantization
- Three language-model families
- Six demographic-bias measurements

It found that acceleration can change bias unpredictably, although its tested KV-cache quantization was generally more stable than weight quantization.

Several newer studies also examine quantization-induced bias, including:

- *Understanding the Effect of Model Compression on Social Bias in Large Language Models* (`arXiv:2312.05662`)
- *How Quantization Shapes Bias in Large Language Models* (`arXiv:2508.18088`)
- *Uncertainty Drives Social Bias Changes in Quantized Large Language Models* (`arXiv:2602.06181`)

Therefore, simply running BBQ or another bias benchmark on quantized models would not be a novel contribution.

## Where We Could Still Add Something

Our narrower question is less explored:

> Does long-context KV token eviction, numerical TurboQuant compression, and their sequential combination amplify or reduce demographic bias on sub-4B models?

The potentially distinctive elements would be:

- KV eviction, not only quantization
- TurboQuant rather than standard HF KV4
- Sequential eviction plus quantization
- Long contexts where the cache is genuinely compressed
- Llama 3.2-3B and Qwen2.5-3B
- Matched configuration comparisons
- Compression-induced changes rather than absolute model bias
- Energy, memory, quality, and fairness considered together

This is a plausible secondary contribution, but not strong enough to justify becoming the central research direction.

## Main Risk

The project already includes:

- AWQ
- PyramidKV-style eviction
- TurboQuant
- Energy monitoring
- Physical storage auditing
- Harder retrieval
- Llama and Qwen
- Packed TurboQuant as a possible extension
- Interaction and Pareto analysis

Adding a large fairness study could make the paper look unfocused:

> One paper attempting energy optimization, cache engineering, retrieval, quantization, social fairness, two models, and custom kernels.

For a strong paper, a coherent central story is usually better than many loosely connected experiments.

## Recommendation

Do **not** make demographic fairness a core requirement for completing the project.

Use it as one of these:

- A small exploratory appendix if the course expects fairness analysis
- A robustness subsection with one established benchmark
- A clearly stated future research direction
- A separate follow-up paper if initial results are interesting

The project’s mandatory priorities should remain:

1. Harder retrieval
2. Matched wrapper control
3. Qwen replication
4. Current TurboQuant reference-path validation
5. Packed TurboQuant attempt
6. Cross-model energy and quality analysis

Only add demographic fairness after those are stable.

## Minimal Useful Fairness Audit

If included, keep it focused.

Use one generation-based benchmark such as `DiscrimEvalGen` or a carefully selected BBQ subset.

Test:

- C1-W
- C2
- C3-R
- C4-R
- C3-P and C4-P only if the packed implementation succeeds

Run it on both Llama and Qwen without power monitoring.

Measure:

- Counterfactual consistency
- Group selection differences
- Refusal rates
- Stereotypical response rates
- Compression-induced changes relative to C1-W

The central metric should be:

```text
Bias change caused by compression
= compressed configuration bias − C1-W bias
```

This avoids claiming that the project can determine whether Llama or Qwen is universally fair.

## Important Cache Detail

A standard short fairness benchmark may not actually test TurboQuant properly.

TurboQuant preserves the most recent 128 tokens in FP16, and the first output token comes from full-prompt processing. A short multiple-choice prompt could therefore bypass most quantized-cache effects.

A valid fairness audit must:

- Use a long enough context to activate cache quantization.
- Place the question at the end.
- Use multi-token generation or inspect answer probabilities after a fixed generated prefix.
- Confirm that the quantized cache was active during the measured decision.

Without these precautions, the experiment could report “no fairness change” simply because the fairness decision never meaningfully used the compressed cache.

## Publication Value

| Fairness addition | Scientific value |
|---|---|
| Small arbitrary demographic prompts | Low |
| Standard benchmark copied without cache-sensitive design | Low |
| Established benchmark with matched configurations | Useful robustness evidence |
| Long-context, cache-sensitive, paired cross-model analysis | Modest secondary novelty |
| Full study across eviction, quantization, interactions, models and benchmarks | Potential separate paper |

For the current project, I recommend a **small, properly designed exploratory audit**, not a major fairness research branch. It can demonstrate responsible evaluation and satisfy instructor expectations, but the primary scientific novelty should remain the implementation-aware interaction between weight quantization, KV eviction, numerical KV quantization, and actual energy behaviour.

## 1. HF QuantizedCache With Optimum-Quanto

**Verdict:** Best fit for the existing Transformers, AWQ, custom-wrapper setup.

### Physical storage

This is genuinely packed at rest:

- INT4 stores two values per `uint8`.
- INT2 stores four values per `uint8`.
- Scales and shifts remain higher precision.
- The configured residual window, normally 128 recent tokens, remains FP16.

The [optimum-quanto `PackedTensor`](https://github.com/huggingface/optimum-quanto/blob/main/optimum/quanto/tensor/packed.py) explicitly packs INT4/INT2 values. This passes a physical-storage test if the test follows the nested `_data` storage rather than trusting the wrapper tensor's public shape or dtype.

### Full-cache dequantization

The persistent cache is compressed, but attention is not performed directly on it. The current [Transformers implementation](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/blob/main/src/transformers/cache_utils.py):

1. Dequantizes all historical K and V for the active layer.
2. Concatenates the FP16 history, residual, and new token.
3. Passes those full-precision tensors to ordinary attention.
4. Requantizes the complete layer every `residual_length` tokens.

Therefore:

- No FP16 copy of every layer persists in the cache object.
- A full FP16 K/V history exists transiently for each active layer.
- The CUDA caching allocator may continue reserving that workspace.
- This is memory compression, not fused low-bit attention.

Quanto can use a CUDA extension for unpacking, but the attention kernel still consumes reconstructed FP16 K/V.

### Compatibility

- Models: generic Cache API makes it suitable for Llama 3.2 and Qwen2.5.
- T4: yes; no Ampere-only instruction is required for cache packing/dequantization.
- AWQ: yes, if the AWQ model remains in standard, unfused Transformers modules.
- Custom attention wrapper: yes, if it calls `cache.update(...)` and consumes returned FP16 tensors.
- Pyramid eviction: not directly. QuantizedCache has no safe token-selection operation for the quantized history.

Use the documented axes:

- Quanto: `axis_key=0`, `axis_value=0`.
- HQQ: `axis_key=1`, `axis_value=1`.

### Package situation

Current published versions found during this review:

- `transformers==5.14.1`
- `optimum-quanto==0.2.7`, requiring `torch>=2.6.0`
- `autoawq==0.2.9`

However, [AutoAWQ is archived](https://github.com/casper-hansen/AutoAWQ) and its maintainer's last tested stack was Torch 2.6.0 and Transformers 4.51.3. Hugging Face separately warns that AutoAWQ may downgrade Transformers to 4.47.1.

The most defensible shared environment to test is therefore:

```text
torch==2.6.0
transformers==4.51.3
autoawq==0.2.9
optimum-quanto==0.2.7
```

Do not use AutoAWQ fused modules. They implement a private preallocated cache and return dummy `past_key_values`, making custom cache replacement invalid. Also explicitly override the Llama AWQ checkpoint's `use_cache: false`.

### Likely energy behavior

At batch size 1, expect:

- Short contexts: almost certainly higher joules due to unpacking, full-history allocation, concatenation, and periodic requantization.
- 8192 tokens: uncertain; VRAM falls, but attention still reads FP16 reconstructed tensors.
- Peak power may decline while runtime increases, so average watts alone would be misleading.

This is scientifically useful as a **physical-at-rest cache compression control**, not evidence that low-bit attention saves energy.

License: Apache-2.0.

## 2. HF QuantizedCache With HQQ

**Verdict:** Useful as a second backend and for INT2, but likely slower and less energy-efficient than Quanto.

### Physical storage

HQQ physically packs its payload:

- Four-bit values use packed `uint8/2`.
- Two-bit values use packed `uint8/4`.
- Three-bit values use packed `int32`.
- Metadata stores scales and zero points.

The implementation is explicit in [HQQ `quantize.py`](https://github.com/mobiusml/hqq/blob/master/hqq/core/quantize.py) and [`bitpack.py`](https://github.com/mobiusml/hqq/blob/master/hqq/core/bitpack.py).

### Execution behavior

It has the same Transformers-level full-history dequantization behavior as Quanto. Additionally, HQQ's default quantizer:

- Promotes inputs to FP32 during quantization.
- Runs its weight optimization path by default.
- Calls `torch.cuda.empty_cache()` during quantization.
- Uses ordinary PyTorch bit unpacking in the Cache path.

Those choices can make periodic cache rebuilding expensive on a T4. The optional HQQ ATen backend primarily concerns HQQ linear layers; Transformers' cache calls the static `Quantizer.dequantize` path.

### Compatibility

- Models: Llama 3.2 and Qwen2.5 through the generic HF Cache API.
- AWQ: yes, unfused only.
- T4: yes, using generic PyTorch CUDA operations.
- Pyramid: same incompatibility as Quanto.
- Package: current `hqq==0.2.8.post1`, requiring `transformers>=4.36.1`.
- License: Apache-2.0.

### Recommendation

Test INT4 first. Treat INT2 as a quality and physical-memory stress point, not an expected energy winner. HQQ is valuable because it demonstrates whether results depend on one packing backend.

## 3. LMDeploy TurboMind INT4/INT8

**Verdict:** Strongest reliable physically compressed and kernel-integrated option, but it changes the inference system.

LMDeploy provides:

- Online asymmetric per-token, per-head KV INT4/INT8.
- Physically packed cache blocks.
- Quantized paged-attention kernels that unpack inside attention rather than materializing a full FP16 history.
- Explicit T4/sm75 support.
- W4A16 AWQ support.
- Llama 3.2-3B and Qwen2.5-3B support.

The [supported-model table](https://github.com/InternLM/lmdeploy/blob/main/docs/en/supported_models/supported_models.md) marks:

- Llama 3.2: KV INT4/INT8 and W4A16.
- Qwen2.5: TurboMind KV INT4/INT8 and W4A16.

Both 3B models have `head_dim=128`, satisfying TurboMind's quantized-cache restriction. The [KV documentation](https://github.com/InternLM/lmdeploy/blob/main/docs/en/quantization/kv_quant.md) explicitly lists T4 and reports four times as many INT4 cache blocks as FP16. The [AWQ documentation](https://github.com/InternLM/lmdeploy/blob/main/docs/en/quantization/w4a16.md) explicitly supports T4 and Hub-hosted AWQ checkpoints.

Current PyPI release: `lmdeploy==0.15.0`. Installation is a single `pip install lmdeploy`, although it should use an isolated Colab runtime because its Torch/Transformers requirements differ from the recommended AutoAWQ stack.

### Energy expectation

This is the only mature option here with a credible mechanism for lower decode energy:

- Less KV DRAM traffic.
- No layer-sized FP16 reconstruction buffer.
- Quantization integrated into cache-fill and attention kernels.

Nevertheless, LMDeploy's published gains are throughput, not joules, and mostly use larger models or high concurrency. At batch 1 with a 3B GQA model, energy savings may still be small.

### Fairness limitations

It cannot be presented as just another C2 implementation because it changes:

- Attention kernels.
- Cache allocator.
- Scheduler.
- AWQ kernels.
- Generation runtime.

Use it as an **external systems upper-bound/control**, not in the same paired statistical family as the Transformers runs.

Pyramid-style token eviction is not exposed through the HF Cache API. Implementing it would require changing LMDeploy's block manager and kernels.

License: Apache-2.0.

## 4. Official KIVI

**Verdict:** Best algorithmic candidate, but not currently a T4 drop-in.

### Strengths

Official KIVI stores packed 2/4-bit historical K/V and uses custom GEMV kernels directly on compressed cache data. Its [Llama implementation](https://github.com/jy-yuan/KIVI/blob/main/models/llama_kivi.py) computes:

- Query times packed keys through `cuda_bmm_fA_qB_outer`.
- Attention probabilities times packed values through the same compressed GEMV path.
- Only a small residual window with ordinary FP16 matmul.

No complete dequantized historical cache persists or is reconstructed.

### Blockers

- Only Llama and Mistral model classes are provided; no Qwen2.5.
- Llama 3 GQA support was added for Transformers 4.43.
- The current Llama path asserts that `config.use_flash=True`.
- Prefill calls FlashAttention 2.
- [FlashAttention 2 officially supports Ampere, Ada, and Hopper, not Turing/T4](https://github.com/Dao-AILab/flash-attention#nvidia-cuda-support).
- Its requirements remain an old Torch 2.1/Transformers 4.36-era environment despite the later 4.43 update.
- AWQ loading is not documented or tested.

The custom decode CUDA appears architecture-generic and should be compilable for sm75. A viable port would replace only prefill with PyTorch SDPA/eager attention and transplant KIVI's packed decode path into a current Llama attention wrapper. That remains substantial custom engineering.

### Pyramid interaction

Arbitrary token eviction is especially difficult for KIVI keys because key quantization groups run along the channel/token-oriented layout. Token removal can break packed groups and their scales. Requantization after every eviction would substantially alter both KIVI and PyramidKV.

License: MIT.

## 5. KVTuner

KVTuner is an interesting ICML 2025 extension of HF QuantizedCache with:

- Separate K and V precision.
- Per-layer and per-head mixed precision.
- Vanilla, HQQ, and Quanto backends.
- Generic HF model loading.

Its [source](https://github.com/cmd2001/KVTuner/blob/master/flexible_quant/flexible_quant/flexible_quantized_cache.py) still dequantizes the complete history for every update, so it has the same energy limitation as HF QuantizedCache. It also relies on older `DynamicCache.key_cache` and `_seen_tokens` internals, making it version-sensitive.

The repository has no top-level license file. That makes redistribution or incorporating its code legally ambiguous. Use the paper/method as inspiration or request licensing clarification before integrating code.

## Options To Reject

### KVQuant official

KVQuant has genuinely packed 2/3/4-bit caches and custom CUDA kernels that operate on compressed data, plus sparse outlier corrections. However:

- It requires Fisher/calibration preprocessing and a generated `quantizers.pickle`.
- It vendors a complete modified Transformers tree.
- Deployment forcibly enables FlashAttention 2.
- Its kernels currently do not support GQA; [the Llama 3 GQA issue remains open](https://github.com/SqueezeAILab/KVQuant/issues/21).
- Both Llama 3.2-3B and Qwen2.5-3B use GQA.
- It has no clear top-level repository license.
- AWQ is not a supported deployment configuration.

Not practical or fair for this study.

### GEAR

GEAR's compressed form is real: packed KIVI data plus low-rank and sparse error recovery. But its official source:

- Implements only a custom Llama path.
- Explicitly asserts `num_key_value_groups == 1`, rejecting both target models.
- Uses Transformers 4.38-era internals.
- Depends on FlashAttention 2.
- Has no packaged integration and a highly environment-specific requirements file.
- Uses online low-rank recovery that is likely expensive at batch 1.

The repository has an MIT file but also a README statement describing the code as non-commercial, creating avoidable licensing ambiguity.

### ExLlamaV2 Q4

ExLlamaV2 physically stores Q4 K/V and uses CUDA quantization, but its [cache source](https://github.com/turboderp-org/exllamav2/blob/master/exllamav2/cache.py) allocates persistent full-size FP16 temporary K/V tensors for one active layer per device. It therefore saves all-layer storage but fails a strict “no full dequantized layer workspace” gate.

It is also:

- Archived in favor of ExLlamaV3.
- EXL2/GPTQ-oriented, not AWQ.
- A separate runtime with no HF Cache or Pyramid wrapper compatibility.

License: MIT.

### vLLM INT4

Current vLLM `main` contains a physically packed `int4_per_token_head` mode with RHT, per-token-head scales, and a dedicated Triton attention kernel. The cache specification explicitly allocates `head_size // 2` bytes for packed INT4.

However:

- Stable documentation still describes only FP8 KV cache.
- INT4 appears in developer/main code rather than as a documented stable feature.
- It supports only causal attention in the current kernel.
- General vLLM supports T4, but T4 validation of this new INT4 kernel was not found.
- It requires a separate vLLM runtime and cannot use the custom HF/Pyramid wrapper.

This is promising for a future external control, not the primary experiment.

## Expected Cache Sizes

At FP16, batch size 1:

| Model | FP16 KV/token | 512 | 2048 | 8192 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Llama 3.2-3B, 28 layers, 8 KV heads | 112 KiB | 56 MiB | 224 MiB | 896 MiB |
| Qwen2.5-3B, 36 layers, 2 KV heads | 36 KiB | 18 MiB | 72 MiB | 288 MiB |

Raw INT4 payload is one quarter of those figures, before scales and the FP16 residual window. This explains why generic HF cache quantization is unlikely to save energy at 512 or 2048 tokens: the cache is too small for memory savings to outweigh repeated full-history dequantization.

## Fair Combination Rules

**Fair with AWQ**

- HF Quanto/HQQ with standard unfused Transformers AWQ modules.
- LMDeploy AWQ plus KV INT4, but only as a separate system-level experiment.

**Not fairly combinable with AWQ**

- ExLlamaV2: different weight format.
- llama.cpp/GGUF: different weight format and runtime.
- KVQuant/GEAR: old custom model classes and unvalidated AWQ loading.
- Official KIVI: potentially portable, but no validated AWQ configuration.

**Not plug-and-play with Pyramid eviction**

- HF QuantizedCache: no token-index selection for quantized history.
- KIVI/KVQuant/GEAR: packed layout and quantization groups require custom compaction or requantization.
- LMDeploy/vLLM: block-managed caches, no Pyramid token-scoring API.
- ExLlamaV2: separate fixed/paged cache manager.

A fair compound method would need one custom cache that defines a fixed ordering, preferably **Pyramid selection first, then quantization**, and reports both retained tokens and actual packed bytes. Simply bolting QuantizedCache onto the existing DynamicCache adapter would not produce a valid compound ablation.

## Recommended Experiment Decision

Use:

- **AWQ + HF Quanto INT4** as the replacement physical-cache alternative.
- **AWQ + HF HQQ INT4**, optionally INT2, as a backend/precision sensitivity check.
- **LMDeploy AWQ + KV INT4** as a separate system-level energy benchmark if time permits.

Do not claim that the HF alternatives implement fused low-bit attention. Report them explicitly as **packed persistent storage with transient FP16 reconstruction**. Keep KIVI as future work unless a T4 SDPA-prefill port and current AWQ integration can be validated. No files were modified.

<task_result>
**Bottom Line**
The safest publishable direction is not “a new KV compressor.” Recent 2026 work already covers joint eviction/quantization, matched-budget compression, and deployable fused implementations. The defensible contribution is a **realization-aware T4 study** distinguishing:

1. Nominal bit rate.
2. Reachable persistent tensor storage.
3. CUDA allocator/VRAM footprint.
4. Temporary materialization overhead.
5. End-to-end latency and energy.
6. Retrieval quality.

A strong paper would combine candidates 1–3 below and use the Llama/Qwen comparison as external validation.

## Ranked Contributions

| Rank | Candidate | Novelty | Feasibility | Coherence |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | Dual-budget eviction-versus-quantization comparison | 4.5/5 | 4.5/5 | 5/5 |
| 2 | TurboQuant algorithm-to-realization audit and break-even map | 4/5 | 5/5 | 5/5 |
| 3 | Factorial non-additivity of sequential compression | 3.5/5 | 5/5 | 5/5 |
| 4 | Cross-model compression portability across contrasting KV geometries | 3/5 | 4/5 | 4.5/5 |

### 1. Dual-Budget Eviction Versus Quantization
**Proposed contribution:** Compare pyramidal eviction and TurboQuant under two explicitly different matching rules:

- **Nominal-rate match:** 4-bit quantization of all tokens versus FP16 retention of approximately 25% of tokens, adjusted for residual windows and metadata.
- **Realized-storage match:** Sweep the eviction capacity until its measured reachable storage matches TurboQuant’s actual persistent reachable storage.
- Report both comparisons rather than treating nominal 4-bit precision as physical 4× compression.

This is particularly valuable when the reference TurboQuant path is numerically correct but retains unpacked or materialized cache tensors. If TurboQuant’s reachable storage is equal to or greater than FP16, report that a lower physical match is infeasible rather than silently substituting theoretical bytes.

**Why it remains novel:** Existing studies generally provide only one side:

- The original TurboQuant evaluation compares methods at a nominal cache ratio of 0.25 but does not establish that the reference cache realizes that ratio physically.
- RDKV evaluates methods under matched FP16-equivalent budgets, but it uses a packed cache and fused decode.
- The July 2026 KV benchmark reports realized compression, but its methods are not strictly memory-matched: SnapKV uses a configured retention ratio while TurboQuant uses 3/4-bit settings.

**Measurements:**

- Theoretical payload bytes.
- Metadata, scales, norms and residual-window bytes.
- Alias-deduplicated reachable tensor storage.
- `memory_allocated`, `memory_reserved`, peak allocation and NVML process memory.
- Prefill and decode latency/energy separately.
- NIAH over multiple depths, needles and haystack seeds.

**Exact caveats:**

- A 4-bit cache is not exactly one quarter of FP16 after scales, norms, codebooks and FP16 residual tokens.
- If full dequantized K/V tensors remain reachable, the result characterizes that implementation, not the compression potential of TurboQuant.
- Your custom method should be called **“pyramidal-budget SnapKV-style eviction”** unless it reproduces official PyramidKV scoring and cache semantics. Do not label its results simply “PyramidKV.”
- Peak VRAM is not a substitute for cache storage because model weights, attention matrices and temporary dequantization buffers can dominate it.

Relevant work: [TurboQuant](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.19874), [RDKV](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.08317), [Benchmarking KV-Cache Optimizations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.05399), [Quantization Dominates Rank Reduction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.11501).

### 2. Algorithm-to-Realization Audit and Break-Even Map
**Proposed contribution:** Treat TurboQuant 0.2 as an auditable research artifact and map four distinct properties:

- **Numerical validity:** reconstruction error, output divergence and retrieval behavior.
- **Representation validity:** index dtype, packing, metadata and residual-window behavior.
- **Residency validity:** whether reconstructed FP16 tensors remain persistently reachable.
- **Deployment utility:** context/output lengths at which latency or energy becomes better than FP16.

The pinned implementation is especially informative: its source stores compressed indices but also constructs and assigns full dequantized `self.keys` and `self.values`. Thus, index packing by itself does not prove that the active cache has reduced residency: [pinned `cache.py`](https://github.com/back2matching/turboquant/blob/4de496d48bff9a7524016f60396aa374a999c887/turboquant/cache.py).

Produce a context-by-decode-length break-even surface, for example:

- Contexts: 512, 2K, 4K, 8K.
- Decode lengths: 32, 128, 512 tokens.
- Outcomes: prefill energy, decode J/token, total energy, latency and live bytes.

**Why it remains novel:** The general systems gap is already known, but an exact, reproducible T4/SLM artifact audit with energy and storage accounting is still useful.

- SAW-INT4 argues that offline compression is insufficient without serving-compatible layouts and fused attention.
- RDKV explicitly states that unpacking to FP16 before attention leaves peak HBM unchanged and adds latency.
- UltraQuant distinguishes TurboQuant as an algorithmic quality anchor from a deployable realization.
- The July benchmark acknowledges using an unpacked TurboQuant representation and warns that memory could improve with packing.

**Exact caveats:**

- Do not claim to discover the general reference-versus-realization problem; several 2026 papers identify it.
- Phrase the result as an audit of the exact version, commit, Transformers version and cache path.
- A negative result is “this realization does not deliver physical compression or energy savings,” not “TurboQuant cannot.”
- The package audit alone is probably workshop/short-paper material. It becomes stronger when paired with candidate 1 and the cross-model validation.
- NVML at 10 Hz is weak for short phases. Synchronize CUDA, integrate timestamped samples, lengthen short phases and report raw and idle-adjusted energy.
- GPU-only NVML energy is not whole-system energy.

Relevant work: [SAW-INT4](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.19157), [UltraQuant](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20474), [RDKV](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.08317), [QServe](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.04532), [Transformers QuantizedCache documentation](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/en/kv_cache#quantized-cache).

### 3. Factorial Non-Additivity of Sequential Compression
**Proposed contribution:** Recast the existing AWQ configurations as a proper 2×2 factorial experiment:

| | No eviction | Eviction |
|---|---|---|
| FP16 KV | AWQ | AWQ + eviction |
| TurboQuant KV | AWQ + TQ | AWQ + eviction + TQ |

For each continuous metric \(Y\), report an interaction term:

\[
I_Y = Y_{E+Q}-Y_E-Y_Q+Y_0
\]

Also use a log-scale interaction for multiplicative quantities such as bytes, latency and energy:

\[
I_{\log Y}=\log Y_{E+Q}-\log Y_E-\log Y_Q+\log Y_0
\]

This tests whether stacking behaves independently, synergistically or antagonistically. Apply it separately to:

- Reachable cache storage.
- Peak temporary storage.
- Prefill latency/energy.
- Decode latency and J/token.
- Retrieval probability.

A particularly coherent mechanism is that eviction may reduce TurboQuant’s Python quantize/dequantize and materialization cost by shortening the surviving cache, even when TurboQuant alone fails to reduce physical residency.

**Prior-work boundary:**

- RDKV already compares joint allocation against staged SnapKV+ZipCache.
- MoE-nD jointly routes eviction and quantization by layer.
- Titanus uses cascade pruning followed by quantization.
- KV Pareto studies interactions between AWQ, KV quantization and chunked prefill.

Therefore, **“first joint eviction plus quantization” is not supportable**. The narrower contribution is phase-resolved **energy and realization interaction on 3B models/T4 using accessible reference implementations**.

**Exact caveats:**

- A 2×2 factorial identifies interaction, not operation order.
- To claim an order effect, both `evict → quantize` and `quantize → evict` must be implemented and evaluated independently.
- Retrieval needs many prompts/depths. A single NIAH success/failure per cell cannot support interaction statistics.
- Binary retrieval should use a logistic model or stratified bootstrap rather than a t-test.
- Because every compressed configuration sits on AWQ, conclusions concern KV techniques conditional on AWQ, not their interaction with FP16 weights.

Relevant work: [RDKV](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.08317), [MoE-nD](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.17695), [Titanus](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.17787), [KV Pareto](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.01953).

### 4. Cross-Model Compression Portability
**Proposed contribution:** Test whether conclusions transfer between similarly sized models with very different KV geometry:

- Llama 3.2-3B: 28 layers, 8 KV heads, head dimension 128.
- Qwen2.5-3B: 36 layers, 2 KV heads, head dimension 128: [official config](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct/blob/main/config.json).

Their nominal FP16 KV bytes per token are approximately:

\[
\text{Llama}=2(28)(8)(128)(2)=114{,}688\text{ bytes/token}
\]

\[
\text{Qwen}=2(36)(2)(128)(2)=36{,}864\text{ bytes/token}
\]

Thus, despite similar parameter counts, Qwen’s nominal KV cache is only about 32% of Llama’s per token. At 8K tokens this is approximately 288 MiB versus 896 MiB. That creates a clean hypothesis: eviction and KV quantization should have a later or weaker energy break-even on Qwen, while Python transformation overhead may remain significant.

**Why novelty is limited but useful:**

- Watt Counts already evaluates these exact two models, including on T4, and models architecture-level energy effects.
- However, it uses 16-bit weights, excludes accuracy, and explicitly leaves quantized workloads for future work.
- KV Pareto covers Qwen/Llama/Mistral with AWQ and KV quantization, but not energy or eviction.
- RDKV includes cross-model results but uses a packed fused realization and does not measure energy.

The contribution is therefore **compression portability conditioned on KV geometry**, not raw cross-model energy benchmarking.

**Exact caveats:**

- Do not attribute differences causally to architecture alone. Training, tokenizer, vocabulary, checkpoint quality and AWQ calibration also differ.
- Run both token-matched synthetic inputs and text-matched real prompts. A shared text prompt produces different token counts.
- Normalize results by generated token, analytical KV byte-token and observed live byte-token.
- Use the same software stack and attention backend. Otherwise model-specific kernels may dominate the comparison.
- T4 is a data-center accelerator; describe it as constrained or edge-like hardware, not as an edge device.

Relevant work: [Watt Counts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.09048), [Towards Sustainable LLM Serving](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.01990), [KV Pareto](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.01953), [RDKV](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.08317).

## Recommended Paper Claim
A defensible central claim would be:

> We present a realization-aware evaluation of KV-cache compression on 3B models and an NVIDIA T4, showing how conclusions about eviction, quantization and their composition change when configurations are matched by measured persistent storage rather than nominal bit rate. We distinguish numerical compression from physically resident and end-to-end useful compression, quantify phase-specific energy interactions, and test transfer across Llama and Qwen models with substantially different KV geometry.

Avoid these claims:

- “First combination of AWQ, PyramidKV and TurboQuant.”
- “First matched-budget eviction-versus-quantization comparison.”
- “TurboQuant provides 4× memory compression” for the current path.
- “Custom PyramidKV” unless it exactly reproduces the official method.
- “Architecture causes the energy difference.”
- “Edge deployment” based solely on a Colab T4.

## Source Caveat
Most of the closest work is recent arXiv preprint literature rather than established peer-reviewed systems work. In particular, the July KV benchmark is an arXiv v1 containing placeholder PVLDB metadata, so it should be cited as a preprint. TurboQuant itself is listed through [ICLR/OpenReview](https://openreview.net/forum?id=tO3ASKZlok); the community Python package is an independent realization, not the authors’ official production implementation.

```
import torch
import sys
import os

# Append the cloned repo to the system path
sys.path.insert(0, os.path.abspath('turboquant-pytorch'))
from turboquant import TurboQuantProd
# Simulate an activation dimension (e.g., d=128)
d = 128
bits = 4 # 3 bits for PolarQuant (MSE), 1 bit for QJL residual correction
device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"
# Instantiate the production quantizer
quantizer = TurboQuantProd(d=d, bits=bits, device=device)
# Generate a mock KV vector simulating a hidden state
mock_kv_vector = torch.randn(1, d).to(device)
# Execute the full quantize cycle
compressed_dict = quantizer.quantize(mock_kv_vector)
print(f"Original Vector Shape: {mock_kv_vector.shape}")
print(f"MSE Indices Shape (Phase 1): {compressed_dict['mse_indices'].shape}")
print(f"QJL 1-Bit Signs Shape (Phase 2): {compressed_dict['qjl_signs'].shape}")
```

## Quantized cache
- `hqq` supports int2, int4, and int8 datatypes.

For the `hqq` backend, we recommend setting the `axis-key` and `axis-value` parameters to `1`.

```py
import torch
from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForCausalLM, QuantizedCache

tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("meta-llama/Llama-2-7b-chat-hf")
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained("meta-llama/Llama-2-7b-chat-hf", dtype=torch.float16, device_map="auto")
inputs = tokenizer("I like rock music because", return_tensors="pt").to(model.device)

out = model.generate(**inputs, do_sample=False, max_new_tokens=20, cache_implementation="quantized", cache_config={"backend": "hqq"})
print(tokenizer.batch_decode(out, skip_special_tokens=True)[0])

## **Quantization Techniques for the KV Cache in Llama 3**
```
pip install git+https://github.com/huggingface/transformers
```

This installation supports both HQQ and Quanto (block-wise) quantization methods.

```
pip install HQQ
```

```
import torch
from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForCausalLM, set_seed, BitsAndBytesConfig

set_seed(1234)  # For reproducibility

prompt = "The best tomato sauce is"

model_id = "meta-llama/Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct"

bnb_config = BitsAndBytesConfig(
        load_in_4bit=True,
        bnb_4bit_quant_type="nf4",
        bnb_4bit_compute_dtype=torch.float16,
        bnb_4bit_use_double_quant=True,
)

tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_id)
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(model_id, quantization_config=bnb_config, attn_implementation="flash_attention_2", torch_dtype=torch.float16, device_map="cuda:0")

inputs = tokenizer(prompt, return_tensors="pt").to(model.device)
outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=150, cache_implementation="quantized", cache_config={"backend": "HQQ", "nbits": 4, "q_group_size": 128, "residual_length": 64, "device":model.device})
result = tokenizer.decode(outputs[0], skip_special_tokens=True)

print(result)
```

## Description

[![@ArkaD171717](https://avatars.githubusercontent.com/u/122476906?v=4&size=48)](https://github.com/ArkaD171717)

[ArkaD171717](https://github.com/ArkaD171717)

opened [on May 25, 2026](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/43576#issue-4515252184)

Issue body actions

### Your current environment

```
vLLM 0.21.0 (pip install)
GPU: Tesla T4 (SM75, Turing) — Kaggle free tier
CUDA: 12.4
OS: Ubuntu 22.04 (Kaggle)
Python: 3.11
```

### 🐛 Describe the bug

Running any model with `--kv-cache-dtype turboquant_4bit_nc` on a T4 GPU crashes immediately during prefill:

```
RuntimeError: FlashAttention only supports Ampere GPUs or newer.
```

The TQ backend has a working SDPA fallback path (`F.scaled_dot_product_attention`) gated behind `if not _HAS_FLASH_ATTN`, but it never activates on CUDA because `is_flash_attn_varlen_func_available()` returns `True` on all CUDA platforms — it checks package availability, not hardware compute capability.

### How to reproduce

from vllm import LLM
llm \= LLM(
    model\="Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B",
    kv\_cache\_dtype\="turboquant\_4bit\_nc",
    enforce\_eager\=True,
    max\_model\_len\=2048,
    gpu\_memory\_utilization\=0.5,
)
\# Crashes during engine init on T4

### Root cause

`turboquant_attn.py` line 60:

\_HAS\_FLASH\_ATTN \= is\_flash\_attn\_varlen\_func\_available()
if \_HAS\_FLASH\_ATTN:
    from vllm.v1.attention.backends.fa\_utils import flash\_attn\_varlen\_func

`is_flash_attn_varlen_func_available()` (in `fa_utils.py`) checks whether the `flash_attn_varlen_func` callable exists in the installed package. On any CUDA system with flash-attn installed, this returns `True` regardless of GPU architecture. FA2 kernels require SM >= 8.0 (Ampere+). On SM75 (T4/Turing), the kernel launch fails at runtime.

### Expected behavior

TQ should fall back to the SDPA prefill path on GPUs that can't run FA2. The fallback path already exists and works correctly — it just needs the capability gate.

### Related issues

-   [\[Tracking\] TurboQuant + Gemma 4 multimodal: 5-gate blocker stack #41403](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/41403) — Gate 6 (FA capability gating) is the same class of bug
-   [\[Tracking issue\]: TurboQuant/HIGGS Attention follow-ups #40069](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/40069) — TQ/HIGGS tracking issue

-    Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

Closes [#43576](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/43576)

## Summary

-   Fix `RuntimeError: FlashAttention only supports Ampere GPUs or newer` when running TurboQuant on T4/Turing (SM75)
-   The SDPA fallback path already exists in the TQ backend but is unreachable on CUDA because `is_flash_attn_varlen_func_available()` unconditionally returns `True`
-   Add a compute capability check: if SM < 8.0, set `_HAS_FLASH_ATTN = False` so prefill routes through `F.scaled_dot_product_attention()`

## Root cause

`is_flash_attn_varlen_func_available()` (in `fa_utils.py`) returns `True` on all CUDA platforms — it checks that the function exists in the flash\_attn package, not that the hardware can actually execute FA2 kernels. FA2 requires SM >= 8.0 (Ampere). On T4 (SM75/Turing), the CUDA kernel launch crashes at runtime.

The TQ backend already has a complete SDPA fallback path gated behind `if not _HAS_FLASH_ATTN` (used for CPU/non-CUDA). This path works correctly on SM75 — it just never executes because the flag is always True on CUDA.

## Changes

**`vllm/v1/attention/backends/turboquant_attn.py`** (8 lines):

After `_HAS_FLASH_ATTN = is_flash_attn_varlen_func_available()`, add a compute capability check. If SM < 8.0 (Turing/Volta), override to `False`. The existing `if _HAS_FLASH_ATTN: from ... import flash_attn_varlen_func` conditional import remains correct — it just won't trigger on pre-Ampere.

## Test plan

-    Tested on Kaggle T4 (SM75) with `Qwen/Qwen3.5-4B` + `turboquant_4bit_nc`:
    -   Engine boots successfully (FlashInfer JIT + Triton decode kernel compile)
    -   Prefill routes through SDPA (`_HAS_FLASH_ATTN = False` confirmed)
    -   Decode routes through Triton TQ kernel (no FA dependency)
    -   Generated coherent text on 2 prompts (40 tokens each)
-    Also tested `Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B` (pure-attention, non-hybrid) with same preset — boots, 1.27M token KV cache, generates correctly
-    Verify no regression on SM80+ (Ampere/Hopper) — capability check only fires on SM < 8.0

## Related issues

-   Partially addresses Gate 6 of [\[Tracking\] TurboQuant + Gemma 4 multimodal: 5-gate blocker stack #41403](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/41403) (TQ + Gemma 4 blocker stack) — the SDPA fallback handles any head\_dim, unlike FA2's 256 cap
-   Related to [\[Tracking issue\]: TurboQuant/HIGGS Attention follow-ups #40069](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/40069) (TQ tracking issue)
-   Builds on [\[Feature\] TurboQuant: support hybrid models and uniform quantization #39931](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/39931) (hybrid model support, merged)

## Code Review

This pull request introduces a check to disable Flash Attention 2 on GPUs with compute capability below 8.0, ensuring a fallback to the SDPA path for older hardware like the T4. Feedback suggests using the vllm.platforms.current\_platform abstraction instead of direct torch.cuda calls to prevent premature CUDA initialization in multi-process environments.

# SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0
